work: Enarratio in Epistolam B. Pauli ad Romanos
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: DE PROLOGO HIERONYMI SUPER EPISTOLAS PAULI.
1.title_en: On the Prologue of Jerome to the Epistles of Paul

paras.t: Secundum Hieronymum, quæritur primo, cur post evangelia, quæ legem perficiunt, in quibus præcepta, consilia atque exempla vivendi plenissime proponuntur, scripsit Apostolus istas epistolas. Cujus rationem assignat Hieronymus, scilicet ut in exordio nascentis seu primitivæ Ecclesiæ, novis causis emergentibus, tam præsentia quam futura vitia exstirparet, inutiles quæstiones excluderet, contra hæreticos quoque armaret Ecclesias : sequens in hoc vestigia Prophetarum, qui post scriptam Moysis legem, libros scripserunt quatenus rediviva populi refrenarent peccata, virtutes instruerent, et ad cultum divinum auditores inducerent suppliciorum comminatione, beneficiorum divinorum commemoratione, præmiorumque sponsione.
paras.en: Following Jerome, it is asked first why, after the gospels, which perfect the law and in which the precepts, counsels and examples of living are set forth most fully, the Apostle wrote these epistles. Jerome gives the reason: that at the outset of the newborn or primitive Church, as new occasions arose, he might root out vices both present and future, shut out useless questions, and also arm the Churches against heretics. In this he followed the footsteps of the Prophets, who after the law of Moses had been written wrote books in order to curb the people's sins as they sprang up again, to build up virtues, and to lead their hearers to the worship of God by threatening punishments, recalling God's benefits, and promising rewards.

paras.t: Deinde quæritur de causa numeri epistolarum. Decem enim scripsit Ecclesiis, quatuor vero discipulis, sicut patebit. Hujus ratio est, ut ostendat utriusque Testamenti plenam esse concordiam, summamque utriusque legis in harum epistolarum scriptura includi. Per decem quippe figuratur Testamentum antiquum, propter Decalogum mandatorum Moysi datum ; per quatuor vero signatur Testamentum novum, propter quatuor evangelia. Decem itaque scripsit epistolas ad Ecclesias, ut demonstraret se non discordare a Moyse ; quatuor vero misit discipulis, quoniam eadem est materia evangeliorum et epistolarum, videlicet documenta et opera Christi. — Porro epistolam ad Hebræos quidam dixerunt non esse Pauli, sed Lucæ, vel Barnabæ, vel Clementis, eo quod, contra ceterarum consuetudinem epistolarum, titulo careat, facundiorque sit. Hoc autem a sanctis doctoribus reprobatur. Tacuit enim Apostolus in illius epistolæ principio nomen suum, ne Hebræi, nomine suo audito, ipsam epistolam spernerent atque rejicerent, quoniam Paulus apud eos habebatur suspectus, tanquam legis destructor. Præterea, mirum non est quod eloquentior fuit in idiomate proprio, id est Hebræo, quam alieno, utpote Græco, quo scriptæ sunt epistolæ ceteræ. Nam et gratia perficit naturam, secundum dispositionem ipsius. Unde donum linguarum, seu gratia sermonis, magis perfecit Apostolum in idiomate proprio quam alieno.
paras.en: Next, the reason for the number of the epistles is asked. He wrote ten to Churches and four to disciples, as will appear. The reason is to show the full concord of the two Testaments, and that the sum of both laws is contained in the writing of these epistles. Ten figures the Old Testament, because of the Decalogue of commandments given to Moses; four signifies the New Testament, because of the four gospels. So he wrote ten epistles to Churches, to show that he did not disagree with Moses; and he sent four to disciples, because the gospels and the epistles have the same matter, namely the teachings and works of Christ. — Some have said that the epistle to the Hebrews is not Paul's but Luke's, or Barnabas's, or Clement's, because, contrary to the custom of the other epistles, it lacks a title [that is, the opening salutation naming the writer], and is more eloquent. But the holy doctors reject this. The Apostle left his name unspoken at the beginning of that epistle so that the Hebrews would not, on hearing it, despise and reject the epistle, since Paul was held suspect among them as a destroyer of the law. Moreover, it is no wonder that he was more eloquent in his own tongue, that is Hebrew, than in a foreign one such as Greek, in which the other epistles were written. For grace perfects nature according to its disposition. Hence the gift of tongues, or grace of speech, perfected the Apostle more in his own tongue than in a foreign one.

paras.t: De ordine quoque epistolarum inquiritur, cur epistola ad Romanos ceteris præordinetur, quum ante ceteras non fuerit edita. Quod ideo factum est, quoniam ista epistola ceteris est profundior ; vel, quia Romani monarchiam orbis tenebant; vel, quia in ista epistola contra primum peccatum, quod est superbia, disputat. In Ecclesia enim Romanorum, mixti erant conversi ex Judaismo et gentilitate, et hi inter se contendebant de dignitate, et quidam eorum propriis meritis se putabant salvandos. Horum ergo errorem atque superbiam reprobans sanctus Apostolus, revocat eos ad unitatem, humilitatem ac pacem, ostendens Judæos legem scriptam, gentiles vero legem naturalem transgressos.
paras.en: The order of the epistles is also inquired into: why the epistle to the Romans is placed before the others, though it was not published before them. This was done because this epistle is deeper than the others; or because the Romans held the monarchy of the world; or because in this epistle he argues against the first sin, which is pride. In the Church of the Romans converts from Judaism and from the Gentiles were mixed together, and they contended among themselves about precedence, and some of them thought they would be saved by their own merits. Rebuking their error and pride, the holy Apostle calls them back to unity, humility and peace, showing that the Jews transgressed the written law and the Gentiles the natural law.

paras.t: Postremo, omnium epistolarum generalis intentio principalisque finis est, ad plenam observantiam evangelicæ doctrinæ, ac per hoc ad vitam æternam inducere. Singulæ quoque epistolæ proprias sortiuntur materias ac proprium finem.
paras.en: Lastly, the general intention and chief end of all the epistles is to lead men to the full observance of the gospel teaching, and through this to eternal life. Each epistle also has its own matter and its own end.

1.title: EXPOSITIO PRIMI CAPITULI EPISTOLÆ AD ROMANOS.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter of the Epistle to the Romans.

paras.t: Paulus, servus Jesu Christi, vocatus apostolus, segregatus in Evangelium Dei, quod ante promiserat per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis de Filio suo, etc. In hac epistola, sicut in conscriptione epistolarum fieri solet, præmittit salutationem : et primo exprimit personam salutantem, id est se ipsum, dicendo : Paulus, servus Jesu Christi. In hoc autem quod ait, Paulus, commendat personam suam a nomine ; quum vero adjungit, Servus, commendat eam a conditione. Commendat quoque eam a dignitate, quum dicit, Vocatus apostolus. Commendat etiam eam ab officio, subdens, Segregatus in Evangelium Dei.
paras.en: [[1:1|Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God.|Paulus, servus Jesu Christi, vocatus apostolus, segregatus in Evangelium Dei]] [[1:2|Which he had promised before, by his prophets, in the holy scriptures,|quod ante promiserat per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis]] [[1:3|Concerning his Son|de Filio suo]], etc. In this epistle, as is usual in the writing of letters, he puts the greeting first: and first he states the person who greets, that is himself, saying: [[1:1|Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ|Paulus, servus Jesu Christi]]. In saying [[1:1|Paul|Paulus]], he commends his person by its name; when he adds [[1:1|a servant|Servus]], he commends it by its condition. He commends it also by its dignity, when he says [[1:1|called to be an apostle|Vocatus apostolus]]. And he commends it by its office, adding [[1:1|separated unto the gospel of God|Segregatus in Evangelium Dei]].

paras.t: Itaque, Paulus : qui secundum Origenem binomius erat (ad quod allegat illud Actuum : Saulus, qui et Paulus), secundum alios primo appellatus est Saulus, deinde post conversionem dictus est Paulus, id est parvus seu modicus. Sic enim, secundum Augustinum et Bedam, ex humilitate vocavit se ipsum. Secundum Hieronymum autem, dictus est Paulus, a Sergio Paulo, quem convertit. Servus, servitute spontanea, non coacta, servitute caritatis, non puri timoris. De servo enim qui servit solo timore aut solo mercedis intuitu, ait Salvator : Servus non manet in domo in æternum ; et iterum, Jam non dicam vos servos, sed amicos meos. Loquendo autem de servitute amoris, electi sunt servi, quoniam Deo obediunt. Itaque, Servus Jesu Christi : cui servire, regnare est ; et sicut beata Agatha dixit, Summa ingenuitas sive nobilitas est, Christi servum exsistere, atque sub ejus dominio permanere.
paras.en: So then, [[1:1|Paul|Paulus]]: who according to Origen had two names (for which he cites that of the Acts: [[Acts 13:9|Saul, otherwise Paul|Saulus, qui et Paulus]]); according to others he was first called Saul, and then after his conversion was named Paul, that is, small or little. For so, according to Augustine and Bede, he called himself out of humility. According to Jerome, however, he was called Paul from Sergius Paulus, whom he converted. [[1:1|A servant|Servus]], by a willing servitude, not a forced one, a servitude of charity, not of mere fear. For of the servant who serves only from fear or only with an eye to wages, the Saviour says: [[John 8:35|the servant abideth not in the house for ever|Servus non manet in domo in æternum]]; and again: [[John 15:15|I will not now call you servants|Jam non dicam vos servos]], but my friends. But speaking of the servitude of love, the elect are servants, since they obey God. So then, [[1:1|a servant of Jesus Christ|Servus Jesu Christi]]: whom to serve is to reign; and as blessed Agatha said, the highest freedom, or nobility, is to be a servant of Christ and to remain under his lordship.

paras.t: Vocatus apostolus : vocatus, inquam, a Deo, non ab hominibus, id est per gratiam Dei ad apostolatum promotus, atque a Deo immediate in apostolum consecratus. Unde de se ipso hoc modo scribit : Paulus apostolus, non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Jesum Christum et Deum Patrem. Nemo quippe assumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron. Puto autem quod ait, Vocatus apostolus, ex humilitate, quasi dicere volens : Exsistens apostolus, sed vocatus, id est ab hominibus sic æstimatus et dictus, quamvis ego me ipsum non arbitrer dignum apostoli nomine. Ideo namque alio loco fatetur : Ego sum minimus Apostolorum, qui non sum dignus vocari apostolus. Vocatur quoque Paulus per excellentiam quamdam Apostolus, non propter auctoritatem, sed prædicationis efficaciam seu generalitatem. Juxta quod ait : Plus omnibus laboravi.
paras.en: [[1:1|Called to be an apostle|Vocatus apostolus]]: called, I say, by God, not by men; that is, raised to the apostleship by the grace of God, and consecrated an apostle by God immediately. Hence he writes of himself in this way: [[Gal 1:1|Paul, an apostle, not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father|Paulus apostolus, non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Jesum Christum et Deum Patrem]]. For [[Heb 5:4|Neither doth any man take the honour to himself, but he that is called by God, as Aaron was|Nemo quippe assumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron]]. But I think he says [[1:1|called to be an apostle|Vocatus apostolus]] out of humility, as though meaning: not being an apostle, but called one, that is, so esteemed and named by men, although I do not reckon myself worthy of the name of apostle [the Latin *vocatus* can mean both “called” and “so named”]. For this is why in another place he confesses: [[1 Cor 15:9|I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle|Ego sum minimus Apostolorum, qui non sum dignus vocari apostolus]]. Paul is also called *the* Apostle by a certain excellence, not on account of authority, but on account of the efficacy or the universality of his preaching; according to what he says: [[1 Cor 15:10|I have laboured more abundantly than all they|Plus omnibus laboravi]].

paras.t: Segregatus in Evangelium Dei, id est ab aliis separatus, quatenus evangelicam legem annuntiem. Dicitur autem, Segregatus, id est a grege infidelium Judæorum divisus, mente seu fide, loco et corpore. De quibus loquitur : Non acquievi carni et sanguini. Vel, Segregatus a grege Apostolorum et aliorum discipulorum, secundum quod aiebat Spiritus Sanctus : Segregate mihi Paulum et Barnabam in opus ad quod assumpsi eos. Ab his segregatus est corpore, non mentis unione. Denique nomine Dei, hoc loco intelligitur Deus Pater. Subditur enim :
paras.en: [[1:1|Separated unto the gospel of God|Segregatus in Evangelium Dei]], that is, set apart from others, so that I may proclaim the law of the Gospel. And he says *separated* [*segregatus*, literally “set off from the flock”, *grex*], that is, divided from the flock of the unbelieving Jews, in mind or faith, in place and in body; of whom he says: [[Gal 1:16|I condescended not to flesh and blood|Non acquievi carni et sanguini]]. Or, separated from the flock of the Apostles and the other disciples, according to what the Holy Ghost said: [[Acts 13:2|Separate me Saul and Barnabas, for the work whereunto I have taken them|Segregate mihi Paulum et Barnabam in opus ad quod assumpsi eos]] [Denis's text has “Paul” for “Saul”]. From these he was separated in body, not in union of mind. Lastly, by the name *God* is understood in this place God the Father. For it follows:

paras.t: Quod, scilicet Evangelium, ante, videlicet a principio mundi, maxime tamen a tempore Moysis, vel etiam Abrahæ, promiserat, ex sua pietate, non hominum merito, per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis, id est libris a Prophetis conscriptis, de Filio suo unigenito, naturali ac vero, non adoptivo. Adam autem propheta erat : similiter Enoch et Noe. Scripturam vero Enoch allegat Judas apostolus. Et quamvis liber Enoch non inter Scripturas sanctas reputetur, sed inter apocrypha, eo quod perversi aliqua inconvenientia libro illi miscuerint, certum est tamen librum illum, secundum quod ab Enoch editus est, sacram fuisse Scripturam. Et forsitan plures Sancti ante diluvium scripserunt de Christo. Moyses quoque et Josue memoriam faciunt libri Justorum, quem constat esse vetustum, de Evangelio Christi saltem mystice seu figurative loquentem. Hinc etiam Judæorum magistri testantur, quod omnes Prophetæ non sunt locuti nisi super dies Messiæ. Propter quod Petrus in Actibus de Christo loquens : Huic, inquit, omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent ; et iterum, Omnes, ait, Prophetæ a Samuele, prænuntiaverunt dies istos. Sed et ipse Salvator sic loquitur : Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege Moysis et Prophetis et Psalmis de me. De lege autem et Evangelio Christi promissum legimus : Lex a me exiet, et judicium meum in lucem populorum requiescet. Et alius Propheta : Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et feriam domui Israel pactum novum, etc.
paras.en: [[1:2|Which|Quod]], namely the Gospel, [[1:2|he had promised before|ante promiserat]], that is, from the beginning of the world, but above all from the time of Moses, or even of Abraham, out of his own goodness, not through the merit of men, [[1:2|by his prophets, in the holy scriptures|per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis]], that is, in the books written by the Prophets, [[1:3|Concerning his Son|de Filio suo]], his only-begotten, natural and true, not adopted. Now Adam was a prophet; so too Enoch and Noe. And the apostle Jude cites the writing of Enoch[[Jude 1:14||]]. And although the book of Enoch is not reckoned among the holy Scriptures but among the apocrypha, because perverse men mixed some unfitting things into that book, yet it is certain that the book, as it was put forth by Enoch, was sacred Scripture. And perhaps several Saints before the flood wrote of Christ. Moses also and Josue make mention of the book of the Just[[Jos 10:13||]][[2 Kings 1:18||]] [the passage in 2 Kings is not in fact by Moses or Josue], which is known to be ancient, and which speaks of the Gospel of Christ at least mystically or figuratively. Hence too the masters of the Jews testify that all the Prophets spoke of nothing but the days of the Messias. For which reason Peter, speaking of Christ in the Acts, says: [[Acts 10:43|To him all the prophets give testimony|Huic, inquit, omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent]]; and again: [[Acts 3:24|all the prophets, from Samuel and afterwards, who have spoken, have told of these days|Omnes, ait, Prophetæ a Samuele, prænuntiaverunt dies istos]]. And the Saviour himself speaks thus: [[Luke 24:44|all things must needs be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses and in the prophets and in the psalms, concerning me|Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege Moysis et Prophetis et Psalmis de me]]. And of the law and Gospel of Christ we read it promised: [[Is 51:4|a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall rest to be a light of the nations|Lex a me exiet, et judicium meum in lucem populorum requiescet]]. And another Prophet: [[Jer 31:31|Behold the days shall come, saith the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel|Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et feriam domui Israel]], a new covenant, etc.

paras.t: Qui Filius factus, id est natus, est ei, scilicet Deo Patri, utpote ad honorem et gloriam ejus, ex semine, id est posteritate, David prophetæ ac regis, secundum carnem assumptam (de qua dicitur, Verbum caro factum est), id est secundum naturam humanam, quam assumpsit ex Virgine benedicta, ex David progenie orta. Immediatum autem semen corporis Christi, erat purissimus sanguis sacratissimæ Virginis. Si vero sumatur semen pro solito semine quod ceteræ matres in generatione ministrant, videlicet pro superfluo illo naturæ coagulato impuroque sanguine : sic non est natus ex semine virginis Mariæ, quæ quum mundissima fuerit, tale semen non præbuit; sed neque ex semine David, nisi mediate, non immediate.
paras.en: [[1:3|Who|Qui]], the Son, [[1:3|was made|factus, id est]], that is, born, [[1:3|to him|ei]], namely to God the Father, that is, for his honour and glory, [[1:3|of the seed|ex semine]], that is, the posterity, [[1:3|of David|David]], prophet and king, [[1:3|according to the flesh|secundum carnem]] assumed (of which it is said: [[John 1:14|the Word was made flesh|Verbum caro factum est]]), that is, according to the human nature, which he took from the blessed Virgin, sprung from the line of David. Now the immediate seed of Christ's body was the most pure blood of the most sacred Virgin. But if *seed* be taken for the ordinary seed which other mothers supply in generation, namely for that superfluous, coagulated and impure blood of nature, then in this sense he was not born of the seed of the Virgin Mary, who, being most pure, supplied no such seed; nor yet of the seed of David, except mediately, not immediately.

paras.t: Cur autem Apostolus dicit Christum ex semine David factum secundum carnem, et non potius natum? imo et alibi loquitur, Misit Deus Filium suum factum ex muliere : quum tamen ab Evangelista dicatur, Quod ex te nascetur sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei ; et Isaias, Parvulus natus est nobis. Et respondendum, quod ideo, ut ostendat humanam Christi generationem non fuisse naturali et solito modo, sed supernaturali quodam Spiritus Sancti artificio, juxta illud propheticum : Novum creavit Dominus super terram, Mulier circumdabit virum ; et illud, Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te. Verumtamen advertendum, quod licet Christus secundum carnem factus seu natus sit ex semine David, atque ex felicissima Virgine, non tamen simpliciter et absolute conceditur quod Christus sit creatus vel creatura, quoniam non subsistit in esse creato, nec per generationem temporalem adeptus est novam subsistentiam. Et etiam ne videamur aliquo modo communicare Arianis, ceterisque hæreticis, qui Christum dixerunt esse puram creaturam. Ipse equidem est verus Creator ac Deus, et Verbum quod erat in principio, per quod facta sunt omnia. Quum ergo sancti doctores leguntur Christum vocare creaturam, exponendi sunt sapienter.
paras.en: But why does the Apostle say that Christ was *made* of the seed of David according to the flesh, and not rather *born*? Indeed elsewhere too he says: [[Gal 4:4|God sent his Son, made of a woman|Misit Deus Filium suum factum ex muliere]]; whereas the Evangelist says: [[Luke 1:35|the Holy which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God|Quod ex te nascetur sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei]]; and Isaias: [[Is 9:6|a child is born to us|Parvulus natus est nobis]]. The answer is that he does so to show that Christ's human generation was not in the natural and usual manner, but by a certain supernatural workmanship of the Holy Ghost, according to that prophetic word: [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: A WOMAN SHALL COMPASS A MAN|Novum creavit Dominus super terram, Mulier circumdabit virum]]; and that other: [[Luke 1:35|The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee|Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te]]. Yet it must be noted that, although Christ according to the flesh was made or born of the seed of David and of the most blessed Virgin, it is nevertheless not granted simply and absolutely that Christ is created or a creature, since he does not subsist in created being, nor did he acquire a new subsistence [that is, a new personal existence] by his temporal generation; and also lest we seem in any way to side with the Arians and other heretics, who said that Christ was a mere creature. For he is the true Creator and God, and the Word who was in the beginning, by whom all things were made[[John 1:1||]][[John 1:3||]]. When therefore the holy doctors are read calling Christ a creature, they are to be expounded wisely.

paras.t: Præterea Christus Filius Dei Patris, dicitur factus secundum carnem ad gloriam Patris, quia ob id incarnatus et in mundo conversatus est, ut nomen Dei Patris hominibus revelaret, eosque ad cultum ipsius induceret, juxta illud : Ego non quæro gloriam meam, sed glorifico Patrem meum. Et alibi Joannes ait : Pater, manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus; opus consummavi quod dedisti mihi ut facerem. Circa hunc locum sic ait Origenes : Factus est autem Filius Dei, sine dubio quod prius non erat secundum carnem; secundum divinitatem vero erat prius, et non erat quando non erat. — Postremo sciendum quod in Christo sunt duæ generationes seu nativitates, videlicet divina et humana, sed una dumtaxat filiatio. Generatio enim concernit naturam, quæ in Christo duplex consistit; filiatio vero personam, quæ non est nisi una in Christo. Nihilo minus Christus vere est filius Virginis, quia ex ea veraciter natus.
paras.en: Furthermore, Christ the Son of God the Father is said to have been made according to the flesh for the glory of the Father, because he was incarnate and lived in the world for this purpose, that he might reveal the name of God the Father to men and lead them to his worship; according to that: [[John 8:50|I seek not my own glory|Ego non quæro gloriam meam]], but I glorify my Father [the second clause echoes John 8:49]. And elsewhere John says: [[John 17:6|I have manifested thy name to the men|Pater, manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus]]; [[John 17:4|I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do|opus consummavi quod dedisti mihi ut facerem]]. On this place Origen says: “The Son of God was made, without doubt, what he was not before, according to the flesh; but according to the Godhead he was before, and there was no time when he was not.” Lastly, it must be known that in Christ there are two generations or nativities, namely the divine and the human, but only one filiation [sonship]. For generation concerns the nature, which in Christ is twofold; but filiation concerns the person, which in Christ is only one. Nevertheless Christ is truly the son of the Virgin, because he was truly born of her.

paras.t: Qui prædestinatus est Filius Dei in virtute, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, ex resurrectione mortuorum Jesu Christi Domini nostri. Verba hæc difficultatibus plena sunt. Denique de ipsa prædestinatione multa dici possent : quæ infra tangentur. Nunc vero, breviter percurrendo, sciendum quod divina providentia universa complectitur, ita quod Deus gloriosus et sapiens, omnium rerum providentiam habet. Singula namque propter certum finem creavit, eisque desiderium finis impressit, atque de mediis ad finis adeptionem requisitis providit. Quemadmodum vero intellectualis creatura ceteris rebus est sublimior, sic providentia Dei nobiliori modo ei adscribitur, ita quod providentia mentis divinæ, respectu intellectualium creaturarum, prædestinatio dicitur. Est enim prædestinatio, secundum Augustinum, præordinatio alicujus ad gloriam, seu præparatio gratiæ in præsenti, et gloriæ in futuro. In quantum itaque Deus quosdam ad supernaturalem beatitudinem præordinavit, et media perveniendi ad eam dare decrevit ac præparavit, dicitur eos prædestinasse seu præmisisse. Prædestinatio enim est quædam præmissio : talis autem prædestinatio dilectionem ac electionem, secundum modum nostræ conceptionis, præsupponit, et inde procedit. Prædestinatio igitur antecessionem quamdam prædestinantis ante prædestinatum et gratuitum donum includit.
paras.en: [[1:4|Who was predestinated the Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead:|Qui prædestinatus est Filius Dei in virtute, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, ex resurrectione mortuorum Jesu Christi Domini nostri]] These words are full of difficulties. Much could be said of predestination itself, which will be touched on below. For now, running over it briefly, it must be known that divine providence embraces all things, so that the glorious and wise God has providence over all things. For he created each thing for a definite end, impressed on it a desire of that end, and provided the means required for attaining the end. But as the intellectual creature is higher than other things, so God's providence is ascribed to it in a nobler manner, so that the providence of the divine mind with respect to intellectual creatures is called predestination. For predestination, according to Augustine, is the preordaining of someone to glory, or the preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future. Inasmuch, then, as God has preordained certain persons to supernatural beatitude, and has decreed and prepared to give them the means of reaching it, he is said to have predestined them, or *sent them before* [*præmisisse*: Denis plays on *destinare*, “to send”]. For predestination is a kind of sending-before; and such predestination, according to our way of conceiving, presupposes love and election, and proceeds from them. Predestination therefore includes a certain precedence of the one predestining before the one predestined, and a gratuitous gift.

paras.t: Quum ergo sit ita, mirum videtur quomodo nunc sanctus Apostolus dicat, Filium Dei prædestinatum in virtute, etc. Unde, ut fertur, Origenes corrigit litteram, loco prædestinati ponens destinatum, quia ut ait, prædestinatio est nondum entis, destinatio vero est entis. Filius autem Dei est ens æternum. Aliqui quoque sic secernunt textum : Qui prædestinatus (ut ibi sit punctus), est Filius Dei in virtute. Sicque prædestinatus nominaliter sumitur, et est sensus : Qui Filius, exsistens prædestinatus secundum humanam naturam, est Filius Dei unigenitus secundum naturam divinam, in virtute, id est in divina potentia, quæ sibi et Deo Patri communis est.
paras.en: This being so, it seems strange how the holy Apostle can now say that the Son of God was [[1:4|predestinated the Son of God in power|prædestinatum in virtute]], etc. Hence, as is reported, Origen corrects the text, putting *destined* in place of *predestined*, because, as he says, predestination is of what does not yet exist, but destination of what exists; and the Son of God is an eternal being. Some also divide the text thus: *Who, predestined* (with a stop there), *is the Son of God in power*. And so *predestined* is taken as a noun [that is, adjectivally, not as part of the verb], and the sense is: [[1:4|Who|Qui]], the Son, being [[1:4|predestinated|prædestinatus]] according to his human nature, [[1:4|the Son of God|est Filius Dei]], the only-begotten according to his divine nature, [[1:4|in power|in virtute]], that is, in the divine might which is common to him and to God the Father.

paras.t: Verumtamen, quoniam littera nostra habet, Qui prædestinatus est, considerandum qualiter hoc ipsum intelligi debeat. Haymo ergo ita exponit : Qui, id est Christus seu Filius Dei, secundum quod homo prædestinatus est, id est, ejus humanitas prædestinata est et præordinata sine suis meritis, ut esset Filius Dei in virtute, hoc est assumpta a Verbo exsistente in eadem virtute divinitatis cum Patre, et esset unita illi in unitate personæ. Quod vero subjungitur, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, refert Haymo ad illud quod dictum est, Qui factus est ex semine David secundum carnem, ut sit sensus : Filius Dei factus est homo ex semine David secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, id est secundum operationem Spiritus Sancti homines sanctificantis. Ipse enim operatus est hanc superbenedictam Verbi incarnationem seu humanationem. Nam, quamvis facta sit a tota supergloriosissima Trinitate, tribuitur tamen Spiritui Sancto. Unde in Symbolo legitur : Qui conceptus est de Spiritu Sancto. Incarnatio etenim Verbi, est opus summæ pietatis ; pietas autem appropriatur Spiritui Sancto. Quod vero mox sequitur, ex resurrectione mortuorum, refert Haymo ad illud quod dictum est, Prædestinatus est Filius Dei. Eritque sensus : Quod ipse sit Filius Dei, cui natura humana unita est, manifestatum est ex resurrectione mortuorum Jesu Christi Domini nostri, hoc est eorum qui simul cum Christo surrexerunt. De quibus scribit Matthæus : Multa sanctorum corpora qui dormierant, surrexerunt, et venientes in sanctam civitatem, apparuerunt multis. Per hoc enim quod Christus secum mortuos surgere fecit, tanquam ex præclaro miraculo patuit eum esse verum Filium Dei, de cujus passione cecinerunt Prophetæ. Quamvis autem expositio ista sit vera atque catholica, videtur tamen a verbis litteræ aliqualiter aliena. — Ambrosius vero refert prædestinationem hanc Filii Dei, ad manifestationem hominibus factam, qua ab æterno præscitum est ut in tempore manifestaretur esse Filius Dei in virtute.
paras.en: However, since our text has *Who was predestinated*, we must consider how this is to be understood. Haymo expounds it thus: [[1:4|Who|Qui]], that is, Christ or the Son of God, as man, [[1:4|was predestinated|prædestinatus est]], that is, his humanity was predestined and preordained without its own merits, that it should be [[1:4|the Son of God in power|Filius Dei in virtute]], that is, assumed by the Word existing in the same power of the Godhead with the Father, and united to him in unity of person. What is added, [[1:4|according to the spirit of sanctification|secundum Spiritum sanctificationis]], Haymo refers to what was said, [[1:3|who was made to him of the seed of David, according to the flesh|Qui factus est ex semine David secundum carnem]], so that the sense is: the Son of God was made man of the seed of David according to the Spirit of sanctification, that is, by the operation of the Holy Ghost who sanctifies men. For he wrought this more than blessed incarnation, or becoming-man, of the Word. For although it was done by the whole most glorious Trinity, it is nevertheless attributed to the Holy Ghost [by *appropriation*: a work common to the three Persons ascribed to one by a fittingness]. Hence we read in the Creed: Who was conceived of the Holy Ghost. For the incarnation of the Word is a work of supreme goodness, and goodness is appropriated to the Holy Ghost. And what follows straight after, [[1:4|by the resurrection|ex resurrectione mortuorum]] [literally “from the resurrection of the dead”], Haymo refers to the words *was predestinated the Son of God*. And the sense will be: that he is the Son of God, to whom the human nature is united, was made manifest by the resurrection of the dead [[1:4|of our Lord Jesus Christ|Jesu Christi Domini nostri]], that is, of those who rose together with Christ; of whom Matthew writes: [[Matt 27:52|many bodies of the saints that had slept arose|Multa sanctorum corpora qui dormierant, surrexerunt]], [[Matt 27:53|And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, came into the holy city and appeared to many|et venientes in sanctam civitatem, apparuerunt multis]]. For by Christ's making the dead rise with him, it was plain, as from a splendid miracle, that he was the true Son of God, of whose passion the Prophets had sung. But though this exposition is true and catholic, it seems somewhat remote from the words of the text. Ambrose, for his part, refers this predestination of the Son of God to the manifestation made to men, by which it was foreknown from eternity that he should in time be manifested to be the Son of God in power.

paras.t: Sed ut maneamus in ipso textus tenore atque contextu, quantum possibile est, advertendum quod esse prædestinatum competit Christo seu Filio Dei secundum quod homo. Dictum est enim, quod prædestinatio est æterna præordinatio horum quæ per gratiam fiunt in tempore. Quod autem homo est Deus, et Deus homo, in tempore factum est per gratiam unionis, non tantum per gratiam habitualem. Et hoc utique ab æterno fuit præordinatum. Quamvis ergo non concedatur simpliciter, Christus factus est Filius Dei (sensus enim est, quod persona quæ Christus est, facta est Filius Dei, eo quod fieri referatur ad rem secundum quod in se est), hoc tamen conceditur, Christus prædestinatus est Filius Dei esse, quoniam prædestinari convenit rei prout est in apprehensione præordinantis. Persona autem seu hypostasis Verbi apprehendi potest prout in humana natura subsistit. Sed, ut dictum est, prædestinatio ista adscribitur Christo ratione naturæ assumptæ. Nam antecessio et donum gratuitum Christo conveniunt ratione humanitatis dumtaxat.
paras.en: But to keep, as far as possible, to the very tenor and context of the text, it must be noted that to be predestined belongs to Christ, or the Son of God, as man. For it was said that predestination is the eternal preordaining of those things which are done in time by grace. Now that man is God and God is man was brought about in time by the grace of union [that is, the grace by which the human nature is united to the Word in one person], not only by habitual grace; and this was certainly preordained from eternity. Although, then, it is not granted simply that *Christ was made the Son of God* (for the sense would be that the person who is Christ was made the Son of God, since *being made* refers to a thing as it is in itself), yet this is granted: *Christ was predestined to be the Son of God*, since being predestined belongs to a thing as it is in the apprehension of the one who preordains; and the person or hypostasis of the Word can be apprehended as subsisting in human nature. But, as was said, this predestination is ascribed to Christ by reason of the nature assumed. For precedence and gratuitous gift belong to Christ by reason of his humanity alone.

paras.t: Sic ergo exponenda est littera : Qui Filius Dei, scilicet Christus, in duabus naturis subsistens, secundum quod homo prædestinatus est, hoc est, sola gratia seu Dei benevolentia sine propriis meritis præelectus est, non solum ut sit caput Ecclesiæ, et a principio suæ conceptionis in Virgine confirmatus esset in bono et comprehensor perfectus, verum etiam ut esset Filius Dei, non adoptivus, sed naturalis, in virtute, id est divina potestate, per quam prædestinatio ista effectum sortita est, seu ad actum deducta, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, id est per Spiritum Sanctum : quoniam operatione Spiritus Sancti facta est incarnatio Christi, juxta illud, Quod natum est in ea, de Spiritu Sancto est ; incarnatio autem est prædestinationis effectus : secundum Spiritum, inquam, sanctificationis ex resurrectione mortuorum, hoc est secundum Spiritum Sanctum, per cujus sanctificantem gratiam spiritualiter mortui reviviscunt : qui vocantur mortui Jesu Christi Domini nostri, quoniam merito ejus gratiam Spiritus Sancti recipiunt, atque salvantur.
paras.en: The text is therefore to be expounded thus: [[1:4|Who|Qui]], the Son of God, namely Christ, subsisting in two natures, as man [[1:4|was predestinated|prædestinatus est]], that is, was chosen beforehand by grace alone, or the good will of God, without merits of his own, not only to be the head of the Church[[Col 1:18||]], and to be confirmed in good and a perfect *comprehensor* [one who already possesses the vision of God] from the first moment of his conception in the Virgin, but also to be [[1:4|the Son of God|Filius Dei]], not adopted but natural, [[1:4|in power|in virtute]], that is, by the divine might through which this predestination took effect, or was brought into act; [[1:4|according to the spirit of sanctification|secundum Spiritum sanctificationis]], that is, through the Holy Ghost, since the incarnation of Christ was done by the operation of the Holy Ghost, according to that: [[Matt 1:20|that which is conceived in her, is of the Holy Ghost|Quod natum est in ea, de Spiritu Sancto est]]; and the incarnation is the effect of predestination; according, I say, to the Spirit of sanctification [[1:4|by the resurrection|ex resurrectione mortuorum]] of the dead, that is, according to the Holy Ghost, by whose sanctifying grace those spiritually dead come to life again; who are called the dead [[1:4|of our Lord Jesus Christ|Jesu Christi Domini nostri]] because by his merit they receive the grace of the Holy Ghost and are saved.

paras.t: Per quem, scilicet Jesum Christum, accepimus ego Paulus ceterique Apostoli a summa Trinitate, gratiam, id est primitias Spiritus Sancti, seu divinorum munerum supernaturalem infusionem. Gratia autem proprie sumpta, est donum seu habitus supernaturalis, a solo Creatore per creationem infusus, essentiam rationalis creaturæ immediate perficiens, eamque in esse divino ac meritorio statuens. Hæc est gratia gratum faciens, quæ a virtutibus, fructibus ac donis Spiritus Sancti distinguitur. Et apostolatum, id est potestatem seu auctoritatem, præcipuamque commissionem ac legationem prædicandi Evangelium Christi. Ad obediendum fidei, id est ad hoc, ut eos quibus evangelizamus, hortemur et faciamus obedire fidei christianæ, videlicet, ut naturali ratione postposita, intellectum suum humiliter subdant incomprehensibilibus et supernaturalibus testimoniis fidei. Unde inferius ait Apostolus : In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi.
paras.en: [[1:5|By whom|Per quem]], namely Jesus Christ, [[1:5|we have received|accepimus]], I Paul and the other Apostles, from the supreme Trinity, [[1:5|grace|gratiam]], that is, the firstfruits of the Spirit[[Rom 8:23||]], or the supernatural infusion of divine gifts. Grace properly taken is a supernatural gift or habit, infused by the Creator alone by way of creation, immediately perfecting the essence of the rational creature, and establishing it in a divine and meritorious being. This is *sanctifying grace* [*gratia gratum faciens*, grace that makes one pleasing to God], which is distinguished from the virtues, fruits and gifts of the Holy Ghost. [[1:5|And apostleship|Et apostolatum]], that is, the power or authority, and the chief commission and embassy, of preaching the Gospel of Christ. [[1:5|For obedience to the faith|Ad obediendum fidei]], that is, to this end, that we may exhort and bring those to whom we preach the Gospel to obey the Christian faith; namely, that setting natural reason aside, they may humbly submit their understanding to the incomprehensible and supernatural testimonies of faith. Hence the Apostle says further on: [[2 Cor 10:5|bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ|In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi]].

paras.t: Hæc autem accepimus facere in omnibus gentibus, id est ubique terrarum, non solum in una aut paucis nationibus : ut impleremus quod de nobis prædixit Propheta, In omnem terram exivit sonus eorum. Hinc enim Christus aiebat Apostolis : Eritis mihi testes in omni Judæa et Samaria, et usque ad ultimum terræ. Qui etiam per Isaiam de Apostolis loquitur : Mittam ex eis qui salvati fuerint ad gentes in mare, in Africam et Lydiam, tenentes sagittam, in Italiam et Græciam, ad insulas longe ; et annuntiabunt gloriam meam gentibus. Omnia vero hæc fecimus pro nomine ejus, id est pro nomine Christi glorificando ac dilatando, ut omnes convertantur ad ipsum. Denique de Romanis, qui erant Italici, subdit : in quibus, id est inter quas gentes, ad quas missi sumus, estis et vos, Romani, vocati Jesu Christi, id est, vocati a Deo per inspirationem et gratiam ad fidem catholicam, ut sitis Jesu Christi, pertinendo ad oves servosque ejus.
paras.en: And we have received these to exercise them [[1:5|in all nations|in omnibus gentibus]], that is, everywhere on earth, not in one or a few nations only; that we might fulfil what the Prophet foretold of us: [[Ps 18:5|Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth|In omnem terram exivit sonus eorum]]. For this is why Christ said to the Apostles: [[Acts 1:8|you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth|Eritis mihi testes in omni Judæa et Samaria, et usque ad ultimum terræ]]. Who also speaks of the Apostles through Isaias: [[Is 66:19|I will send of them that shall be saved, to the Gentiles into the sea, into Africa, and Lydia them that draw the bow: into Italy, and Greece, to the islands afar off, to them that have not heard of me, and have not seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory to the Gentiles|Mittam ex eis qui salvati fuerint ad gentes in mare, in Africam et Lydiam, tenentes sagittam, in Italiam et Græciam, ad insulas longe ; et annuntiabunt gloriam meam gentibus]]. And all this we have done [[1:5|for his name|pro nomine ejus]], that is, for the glorifying and spreading of the name of Christ, that all may be converted to him. Then, of the Romans, who were Italians, he adds: [[1:6|Among whom|in quibus]], that is, among which nations, to which we have been sent, [[1:6|are you also|estis et vos]], O Romans, [[1:6|the called of Jesus Christ|vocati Jesu Christi]], that is, called by God through inspiration and grace to the catholic faith, that you may be Jesus Christ's, belonging to his sheep and servants.

paras.t: In Evangelio scriptum est, quemadmodum Christus vocaverit ad se duodecim […] discipulos, eos appellans Apostolos, quibus et ait : Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi? quomodo ergo nunc dictum est Apostolos accepisse apostolatum a Deo Trinitate per Jesum Christum? Et respondendum, quod apostolatus, qui est gratia gratis data, et gratia gratum faciens, sunt quidem a Deo, et etiam a Christo secundum quod Deus est, auctoritative, primo et principaliter. A Christo autem secundum quod mediator est Dei et hominum, sunt mediate et exsecutive, seu dispositive, et quodammodo instrumentaliter. Per Christum enim seu per meritum ejus, omnia divinarum munera gratiarum nobis præstantur, secundum quod ipse testatur : Quidquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Propter quod in conclusionibus Orationum Ecclesiæ communiter dicitur : Per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum.
paras.en: It is written in the Gospel how Christ called to him twelve […] disciples, naming them Apostles[[Luke 6:13||]], to whom he also said: [[John 6:71|Have not I chosen you twelve?|Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi]]? [the margin notes here are illegible; Luke 6:13 and John 6:71 fit the words] How then is it now said that the Apostles received the apostleship from God the Trinity through Jesus Christ? The answer is that the apostleship, which is a *grace freely given* [*gratia gratis data*, a gift given for the good of others], and sanctifying grace are indeed from God, and also from Christ as he is God, by authority, first and principally; but from Christ as he is [[1 Tim 2:5|mediator of God and men|mediator est Dei et hominum]] they are mediately and executively, or dispositively, and in a certain manner instrumentally. For through Christ, or through his merit, all the gifts of divine graces are bestowed on us, as he himself testifies: [[John 16:23|if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you|Quidquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis]]. For which reason the Church's prayers commonly conclude: Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

paras.t: Omnibus qui sunt Romæ dilectis Dei, id est a Deo æternaliter præamatis : ipse enim prior dilexit nos; vocatis sanctis, id est fidelibus per divinæ vocationis gratiam sanctificatis, qui etiam veraciter sancti appellantur.
paras.en: [[1:7|To all that are at Rome, the beloved of God|Omnibus qui sunt Romæ dilectis Dei]], that is, loved beforehand by God from eternity: [[1 John 4:10|he hath first loved us|ipse enim prior dilexit nos]] [the words are nearer 1 John 4:19]; [[1:7|called to be saints|vocatis sanctis]], that is, to the faithful sanctified through the grace of the divine calling, who are also truly called saints.

paras.t: Gratia, de qua nunc factus est sermo, quæ est principium omnis actionis meritoriæ, ponens animam in esse spirituali et grato, vobis, et pax interna, quæ est tranquillitas mentis, et quies in debita interiorum ordinatione consistens, de qua Propheta, Non est (inquit) pax impiis, dicit Dominus; et in Psalmo, Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam : præstetur et insit vobis a Deo Patre nostro, qui est Pater Christi per naturam, et Pater noster per gratiæ infusionem, sive adoptionem : de quo Christus in Evangelio, Ascendo ad Patrem meum et Patrem vestrum. Quum ergo sit Pater noster, cum omni fiducia ab eo gratiam postulare debemus, quia ut indulgentissimus pater, libenter tribuet egenis mendicisque filiis quidquid rationabiliter petunt ac jugiter. Ideo namque in Evangelio ait Salvator : Si vos, quum sitis mali, nostis bona data dare filiis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester cœlestis dabit spiritum bonum petentibus se? Et Domino Jesu Christo. Ex hoc arguitur Christum esse verum Deum, quum nullus sit actor aut dator pacis internæ et gratiæ, nisi Deus omnipotens. Sequitur quoque, Deum Patrem et Christum esse unum ac idem causale principium pacis et gratiæ, quoniam solus Creator est causa hujus pacis et gratiæ. Unde constat utriusque esse eamdem deitatem, eamdemque virtutem et operationem, juxta illud : Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit. Et idem rite sentitur de Spiritu Sancto, qui hic non exprimitur, quoniam Patre et Filio nominatis, intelligitur tanquam amor et nexus osculumque amborum.
paras.en: [[1:7|Grace|Gratia]], of which we have just spoken, which is the principle of every meritorious act, setting the soul in a spiritual and pleasing being, [[1:7|to you and peace|vobis, et pax]], inward peace, which is tranquillity of mind and rest consisting in the due ordering of the inner powers; of which the Prophet says: [[Is 48:22|There is no peace to the wicked, saith the Lord|Non est (inquit) pax impiis, dicit Dominus]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]; be granted and dwell in you [[1:7|from God our Father|a Deo Patre nostro]], who is the Father of Christ by nature, and our Father by the infusion of grace, or adoption; of whom Christ says in the Gospel: [[John 20:17|I ascend to my Father and to your Father|Ascendo ad Patrem meum et Patrem vestrum]]. Since then he is our Father, we ought to ask grace of him with all confidence, because as a most indulgent father he will gladly give to his needy and begging sons whatever they ask reasonably and constantly. For this is why the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:13|If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to them that ask him?|Si vos, quum sitis mali, nostis bona data dare filiis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester cœlestis dabit spiritum bonum petentibus se?]]? [[1:7|And from the Lord Jesus Christ|Et Domino Jesu Christo]]. From this it is argued that Christ is true God, since no one is the author or giver of inward peace and of grace except almighty God. It follows also that God the Father and Christ are one and the same causal principle of peace and grace, since the Creator alone is the cause of this peace and grace. Hence it is plain that both have the same Godhead, and the same power and operation, according to that: [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]]. And the same is rightly held of the Holy Ghost, who is not expressed here, because when the Father and the Son are named, he is understood as the love, the bond and the kiss of both.

paras.t: Præmissa persona scribentis, et eis quibus scribitur commemoratis, forma quoque salutationis præhabita, sequitur narratio. Primum quidem, id est ante cetera quæ dicturus sive acturus sum; vel, Primum, id est præcipue ; gratias ago Deo meo, simplici in essentia, et trino in Personis : qui licet sit omnium Deus ratione creationis, est tamen specialiter Deus meus, propter singularem caritatem et pietatem ejus super me; et item propter præcipuam spem, dilectionem ac cultum quibus ei inhæreo, dicens cum Psalmista : Deus cordis mei et pars mea Deus in æternum. Solet autem Apostolus (et ita fieri decet) a gratiarum actione incipere. Per Jesum Christum, secundum quod homo est et Dei ac hominum mediator : ita quod Christus est mihi causa gratias agendi Deo meo, quoniam beneficia ejus, et omnia quæ ipse pro nobis fecit ac pertulit, excitant et obligant me ad gratias Deo altissimo referendas, qui tanta bona hominibus per Christum largitus est. Pro omnibus vobis, id est propter beneficia Dei vobis collata; vel, Pro omnibus vobis, id est pro vestro profectu atque salute, quatenus me pro vobis gratias referente, augeatur in vobis salus et gratia Christi; vel, Pro omnibus vobis, supplendo vestrum imperfectum; vel, Pro omnibus vobis, id est in persona omnium vestrum, seu vice vestra. Quia fides vestra annuntiatur in universo mundo, id est in multis ac principalibus finibus mundi. Romani enim, quoniam toti mundo præsidebant, famosissimi erant, et ideo fides eorum per omnia ora fidelium volitabat. Dixerunt enim aliæ Ecclesiæ gentium : Ecce Roma, quæ est caput ac domina mundi, fidem suscepit. Sicque confirmabantur in fide exemplo fidei Romanorum.
paras.en: The person of the writer having been set down, those to whom he writes mentioned, and the form of greeting given, the narrative follows. [[1:8|First|Primum quidem]], that is, before the other things I am about to say or do; or, *first*, that is, chiefly; [[1:8|I give thanks to my God|gratias ago Deo meo]], simple in essence and threefold in Persons: who, though he is God of all by reason of creation, is yet especially my God, because of his singular charity and goodness towards me; and also because of the special hope, love and worship by which I cleave to him, saying with the Psalmist: [[Ps 72:26|thou art the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever|Deus cordis mei et pars mea Deus in æternum]]. Now the Apostle is accustomed (and it is fitting so to do) to begin with thanksgiving. [[1:8|Through Jesus Christ|Per Jesum Christum]], as he is man and mediator of God and men: so that Christ is to me the cause of giving thanks to my God, since his benefits, and all that he did and suffered for us, rouse and bind me to render thanks to the most high God, who has bestowed such great good things on men through Christ. [[1:8|For you all|Pro omnibus vobis]], that is, because of God's benefits conferred on you; or, *for you all*, that is, for your progress and salvation, so that through my giving thanks for you, the salvation and grace of Christ may be increased in you; or, *for you all*, supplying what is lacking in you; or, *for you all*, that is, in the person of you all, or in your stead. [[1:8|because your faith is spoken of in the whole world|Quia fides vestra annuntiatur in universo mundo]], that is, in many and the chief regions of the world. For the Romans, since they ruled the whole world, were most famous, and so their faith flew through all the mouths of the faithful. For the other churches of the Gentiles said: Behold, Rome, which is the head and mistress of the world, has received the faith. And so they were confirmed in the faith by the example of the Romans' faith.

paras.t: In his verbis commendatur nobis caritas sancti Apostoli, qui de proximorum salute sicut de propria exsultavit et gratias retulit. Ita et nos agere competit, ut scilicet gratias Deo agamus, quum audimus aut scimus proximos nostros spiritualiter prosperari. Unde infra scriptum est : Gratias agentes Deo pro omnibus semper. Asserit quoque Apostolus se gratias agere de fide Romanorum, quoniam fides fundamentum est universarum virtutum. In fide tamen includit cetera dona gratiæ Dei.
paras.en: In these words the charity of the holy Apostle is commended to us, who rejoiced and gave thanks for the salvation of his neighbours as for his own. So too it befits us to do, namely to give thanks to God when we hear or know that our neighbours prosper spiritually. Hence it is written further on: [[Eph 5:20|Giving thanks always for all things, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God|Gratias agentes Deo pro omnibus semper]]. The Apostle also says that he gives thanks for the faith of the Romans because faith is the foundation of all the virtues; yet in faith he includes the other gifts of God's grace.

paras.t: Testis enim mihi est Deus, cui servio cultu latriæ in spiritu meo, id est in superioribus viribus animæ meæ, videlicet : in intellectu, credendo, orando, contemplando ; et voluntate, sperando, amando, et cetera bona opera agendo ; in Evangelio Filii ejus, quod aliis prædico, cui obedio, et pro quo multa sustineo. Evangelium autem Filii Dei seu Christi, est annuntiatio bona, et sancta doctrina, quam Christus primo edocuit, et per Apostolos aliis nuntiavit. Hoc loco, sicut et alias sæpe, jurat Apostolus, quatenus melius sibi credatur. Quod fecit propter infirmitatem eorum quibus loquebatur. Nec tamen fecit contra illud Salvatoris in Evangelio : Ego dico vobis, non jurare omnino ; et iterum : Sit sermo vester, Est, est, Non, non. Unde et Jacobus dicit : Ante omnia nolite jurare. His enim verbis prohibetur juratio falsa, consulitur jurationis dissuefactio, permittitur juratio necessaria. Propter quod Christus adjecit : Quod amplius est, a malo est. Non dixit, Malum est, sed, A malo est, id est ab imperfectione vel incredulitate ejus propter quem juratio adhibetur. Imo juratio debite circumstantionata, est actus virtutis quæ latria nuncupatur. Unde scriptum est : Dominum Deum tuum timebis, et per nomen ejus jurabis ; et in Psalmo, Laudabuntur omnes qui jurant in eo.
paras.en: [[1:9|For God is my witness, whom I serve|Testis enim mihi est Deus, cui servio]] with the worship of *latria* [the worship due to God alone] [[1:9|in my spirit|in spiritu meo]], that is, in the higher powers of my soul, namely: in the intellect, by believing, praying, contemplating; and in the will, by hoping, loving, and doing other good works; [[1:9|in the gospel of his Son|in Evangelio Filii ejus]], which I preach to others, which I obey, and for which I endure many things. Now the Gospel of the Son of God, or of Christ, is the good tidings and holy doctrine which Christ first taught, and announced to others through the Apostles. In this place, as often elsewhere, the Apostle swears, that he may be the better believed; which he did because of the weakness of those to whom he spoke. Yet he did not act against that saying of the Saviour in the Gospel: [[Matt 5:34|I say to you not to swear at all|Ego dico vobis, non jurare omnino]]; and again: [[Matt 5:37|let your speech be yea, yea: no, no|Sit sermo vester, Est, est, Non, non]]. Hence James also says: [[Jas 5:12|above all things, my brethren, swear not|Ante omnia autem, fratres mei, nolite jurare]]. For by these words false swearing is forbidden, the giving up of the habit of swearing is counselled, and necessary swearing is permitted. For which reason Christ added: [[Matt 5:37|that which is over and above these, is of evil|Quod amplius est, a malo est]]. He did not say, *It is evil*, but *It is of evil*, that is, from the imperfection or unbelief of him for whose sake the oath is used. Nay, an oath taken with due circumstances is an act of the virtue called *latria*. Hence it is written: [[Deut 6:13|Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve him only, and thou shalt swear by his name|Dominum Deum tuum timebis, et per nomen ejus jurabis]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 62:12|all they shall be praised that swear by him|Laudabuntur omnes qui jurant in eo]] [the margin gives Ps. lxii, 12].

paras.t: Hujus itaque rei testis est mihi Deus, quod sine intermissione, id est omnibus congruis horis seu aptis temporibus, memoriam vestri facio, id est, vestri reminiscor, et coram Deo memor sum vestri, semper, id est in omni tempore convenienti : juxta quem sensum ait Salvator, Oportet semper orare, et non deficere; in orationibus meis. Ex isto elucescit, quod interdum licet et expedit ut unus alii manifestet dilectionem, sollicitudinem et laborem, quibus pro ipso afficitur et fatigatur, non ad accipiendum humanum favorem, aut temporalem mercedem, sed ut alius ex hoc ad meliora provocetur, atque de proximo suo melius sentiat et confidat. Quod tunc maxime fieri debet, quum unus de alio sinistre aut impie suspicatur. Obsecrans, hoc est, per sacrorum commemorationem orans : sicut quum dicitur, Per passionem tuam libera nos ; si quo modo, id est ut aliquo modo, tandem aliquando, post multa ac longa desideria, prosperum iter habeam in voluntate Dei, hoc est secundum divinæ voluntatis beneplacitum : non enim illud absolute oro aut appeto, nisi divina voluntate supposita, semper dicens, Fiat voluntas tua ; veniendi ad vos, o Romani. Nam et ideo creditur Paulus Cæsarem appellasse, etc., quatenus occasionem haberet veniendi Romam.
paras.en: Of this thing, then, God is my witness, [[1:9|that without ceasing|quod sine intermissione]], that is, at all fitting hours or suitable times, [[1:9|I make a commemoration of you|memoriam vestri facio]], that is, I remember you, and am mindful of you before God, [[1:10|Always|semper]], that is, at every convenient time: in which sense the Saviour says: [[Luke 18:1|that we ought always to pray and not to faint|Oportet semper orare, et non deficere]]; [[1:10|in my prayers|in orationibus meis]]. From this it shines out that it is sometimes lawful and expedient for one person to make known to another the love, care and labour with which he is moved and wearied for him, not to win human favour or temporal reward, but that the other may thereby be stirred to better things, and may think better of his neighbour and trust him. This should be done above all when one suspects another wrongly or unkindly. [[1:10|making request|Obsecrans]], that is, praying by the remembrance of holy things [*obsecrare*, from *ob* and *sacra*, “by sacred things”], as when we say: By thy passion deliver us; [[1:10|if by any means|si quo modo]], that is, that in some way, [[1:10|now at length|tandem aliquando]], after many and long desires, [[1:10|I may have a prosperous journey, by the will of God|prosperum iter habeam in voluntate Dei]], that is, according to the good pleasure of the divine will; for I do not pray for or seek this absolutely, but with the divine will presupposed, always saying: [[Matt 6:10|Thy will be done|Fiat voluntas tua]] [the margin reads Matth. x, 10; the words are at Matt 6:10]; [[1:10|to come unto you|veniendi ad vos]], O Romans. For it is believed that Paul appealed to Caesar[[Acts 25:11||]], etc., for this very reason, that he might have occasion of coming to Rome.

paras.t: Desidero enim videre vos, ut aliquid impertiar vobis gratiæ spiritualis, id est, gratiam mihi collatam vobis communicem, instruendo vos plenius de evangelica lege, et disponendo corda vestra per meam exhortationem ad abundantiora dona Spiritus Sancti : quemadmodum Petrus monet, Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei. Non enim debet homo, præsertim prælatus, prædicator, aut doctor, talentum sibi concessum abscondere, quia ut in Ecclesiastico habetur : Sapientia abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque? Ad confirmandos vos in veritate fidei, et observatione evangelicæ legis.
paras.en: [[1:11|For I long to see you that I may impart unto you some spiritual grace|Desidero enim videre vos, ut aliquid impertiar vobis gratiæ spiritualis]], that is, that I may share with you the grace conferred on me, instructing you more fully in the law of the Gospel, and disposing your hearts by my exhortation for more abundant gifts of the Holy Ghost; as Peter admonishes: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another: as good stewards of the manifold grace of God|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei]]. For a man, especially a prelate, preacher or teacher, ought not to hide the talent granted him, since, as is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:32|Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is not seen: what profit is there in them both?|Sapientia abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque?]] [the margin reads Eccli. xvii, 17 (?); the words are at Ecclus 20:32 and 41:17]? [[1:11|to strengthen you|Ad confirmandos vos]] in the truth of the faith and in the observance of the Gospel law.

paras.t: Id est simul consolari in vobis, hoc est, ad hoc cupio vobis gratiam impertiri, ut ex vestra confirmatione, ego quoque in vestro profectu consoler et gaudeam : quoniam sicut de vestra imperfectione contristor, ita de vestra perfectione jucundor ; per eam quæ invicem est, fidem vestram atque meam, hoc est per communem ac mutuam fidem nostram : quæ est fides catholica, in qua fundatur, et ex qua oritur consolatio, qua unus fidelium de profectu et bono alterius consolatur. Hæc quippe consolatio fundatur in hoc, quod credimus et speramus simul ad æternam felicitatem pertingere. Loquitur autem de fide formata, quæ per dilectionem operatur, non de fide informi.
paras.en: [[1:12|That is to say, that I may be comforted together in you|Id est simul consolari in vobis]], that is, I desire to impart grace to you for this, that from your being strengthened I too may be comforted and rejoice in your progress; for as I am saddened by your imperfection, so I am gladdened by your perfection; [[1:12|by that which is common to us both, your faith and mine|per eam quæ invicem est, fidem vestram atque meam]], that is, by our common and mutual faith: which is the catholic faith, on which is founded, and from which springs, the comfort by which one of the faithful is comforted by the progress and good of another. For this comfort is founded on this, that we believe and hope to attain together to eternal happiness. And he speaks of *formed* faith, which works by charity, not of *unformed* faith [that is, faith without charity].

paras.t: Nolo enim vos ignorare, fratres, quia sæpe proposui venire ad vos, si tamen Deus permitteret, et prohibitus sum, id est, impeditus, vel ex divina revelatione vetitus sum ab exsecutione propositi mei, usque adhuc quum præsentem scribo epistolam. Impeditus autem fuit Apostolus per captivitatem seu aliam occupationem. Vel propter Romanorum peccata nondum permisit eum Christus pergere Romam, quomodo in Actibus legitur : Vetati sunt Paulus et sui a Spiritu Sancto loqui verbum Dei in Asia ; et non permisit eos Spiritus Jesu. Postea tamen prædicavit Paulus in Asia.
paras.en: [[1:13|And I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that I have often purposed to come unto you|Nolo enim vos ignorare, fratres, quia sæpe proposui venire ad vos]], if only God would permit, [[1:13|and have been hindered|et prohibitus sum]], that is, prevented, or forbidden by divine revelation from carrying out my purpose, [[1:13|hitherto|usque adhuc]], now when I write the present epistle. The Apostle was prevented by captivity or some other occupation. Or, because of the Romans' sins, Christ did not yet allow him to go to Rome; as we read in the Acts: [[Acts 16:6|forbidden by the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia|Vetati sunt Paulus et sui a Spiritu Sancto loqui verbum Dei in Asia]] [Denis has “Paul and his companions”]; [[Acts 16:7|and the Spirit of Jesus suffered them not|et non permisit eos Spiritus Jesu]]. Yet afterwards Paul preached in Asia[[Acts 19:10||]].

paras.t: Ideo autem proposui venire ad vos, ut aliquem fructum habeam in vobis, id est, spiritualem profectum in vobis producam, vosque in gratia Dei ac bonis operibus fructificare faciam, et etiam ut vobis prædicando, majus meritum in præsenti, majusque præmium in futuro acquiram : quæ omnia finaliter refero ad gloriam Dei sublimis ac omnipotentis ; sicut et in ceteris gentibus quibus prædicavi, fructum aliquem habeo. Græcis qui naturali ingenio pollent, et philosophiæ inventores fuerunt, ac Barbaris, id est hominibus duris, et quasi sine lege viventibus (omnes autem præter Latinos, Hebræos et Græcos, Barbari appellantur), sapientibus et insipientibus, id est fidelibus et infidelibus, doctis et indoctis, unum Deum verum noscentibus, et idola venerantibus, debitor sum prædicare eis Evangelium regni cœlestis, non propter eorum merita, aut dona ab eis recepta, sed ex commissione divina, et propter beneficia mihi divinitus condonata, quæ ordinantur ad hoc ut omnibus prædicem. Gratiæ enim gratis datæ, ordinantur ad proximum. Ita quod in me promptum est, id est, sic quod ego ob hanc obligationem, magis tamen ex caritate, paratus sum et vobis qui Romæ estis, evangelizare.
paras.en: And I purposed to come to you for this, [[1:13|that I might have some fruit among you|ut aliquem fructum habeam in vobis]], that is, that I may produce spiritual progress in you and make you bear fruit in the grace of God and in good works, and also that by preaching to you I may gain greater merit in the present and a greater reward in the future: all of which I refer finally to the glory of God, most high and almighty; [[1:13|even as among other Gentiles|sicut et in ceteris gentibus]] to whom I have preached I have some fruit. [[1:14|To the Greeks|Græcis]], who excel in natural talent and were the inventors of philosophy, [[1:14|and to the barbarians|ac Barbaris]], that is, to rough men living as though without law (for all except the Latins, Hebrews and Greeks are called barbarians), [[1:14|to the wise and to the unwise|sapientibus et insipientibus]], that is, to the faithful and the unbelieving, the learned and the unlearned, those who know the one true God and those who worship idols, [[1:14|I am a debtor|debitor sum]] to preach to them the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom, not because of their merits or gifts received from them, but by divine commission, and because of the benefits bestowed on me by God, which are ordered to this, that I should preach to all. For graces freely given are ordered to the neighbour. [[1:15|So (as much as is in me) I am ready|Ita quod in me promptum est]], that is, so that I, because of this obligation, but still more out of charity, am ready [[1:15|to preach the gospel to you also that are at Rome|et vobis qui Romæ estis, evangelizare]].

1.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS HUJUS PRIMI CAPITULI, AB EO LOCO QUO DICITUR : NON ENIM ERUBESCO EVANGELIUM.
1.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this first chapter, from the place where it says: For I am not ashamed of the Gospel.

paras.t: Merito dixi me esse paratum evangelizare et vobis Romanis : Non enim erubesco Evangelium, hoc est, non confundor publice annuntiare crucem et passionem ac cetera mysteria Christi, quæ in Evangelio describuntur, atque a reprobis irridentur. Paratus sum namque pro nomine Jesu contumeliam pati, quoniam ipse ait : Qui me erubuerit et meos sermones, hunc Filius hominis erubescet, quum venerit in regno suo. Huic consonat illud Psalmistæ : Et loquebar in testimoniis tuis in conspectu regum, et non confundebar. Ratio hujus subjicitur : Virtus enim Dei est in salutem omni credenti, hoc est, Evangelium Christi est virtus, id est potens effectus divinæ potestatis, seu fortis doctrina, proficiens in salutem æternam omni credenti per fidem formatam ac perseverantem, Judæo primum, hoc est ex Judaismo conversis, videlicet primitivæ Ecclesiæ, quæ ex Judæis constabat. Nam et Christus dicebat : Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel, hoc est, ad Synagogam primo ac principaliter missus sum. Ideo Paulus aiebat Judæis : Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei. Deinde et Græco, hoc est ex gentilitate conversis, valet Evangelium. Per Græcos, quasi a digniori, gentiles significat. Repulsa enim prædicatione Apostolorum a Judæis, justa facta est transmigratio ad gentiles, secundum quod Paulus testatur : Quia repulistis illud, et indignos vos judicastis vitæ æternæ, ecce convertimur ad gentes. Secundum Haymonem, Evangelium dicitur virtus Dei, quoniam Christum Dei virtutem annuntiat. Secundum Ambrosium vero, dicitur virtus Dei, quoniam valet ad indulgentiam peccatorum, et ad operationem miraculorum.
paras.en: Rightly have I said that I am ready to preach the gospel to you Romans also: [[1:16|For I am not ashamed of the gospel|Non enim erubesco Evangelium]], that is, I am not abashed to proclaim publicly the cross and passion and the other mysteries of Christ which are described in the Gospel and are mocked by the reprobate. For I am ready to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus[[Acts 5:41||]], since He Himself says: [[Luke 9:26|he that shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of man shall be ashamed|Qui me erubuerit et meos sermones, hunc Filius hominis erubescet]], when he shall come in his kingdom. With this agrees that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 118:46|And I spoke of thy testimonies before kings: and I was not ashamed|Et loquebar in testimoniis tuis in conspectu regum, et non confundebar]]. The reason of this is added: [[1:16|For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth|Virtus enim Dei est in salutem omni credenti]], that is, the Gospel of Christ is power, that is, a mighty effect of the divine might, or a strong teaching, availing unto eternal salvation for every one who believes with a faith that is formed [that is, quickened by charity] and persevering; [[1:16|to the Jew first|Judæo primum]], that is, to those converted from Judaism, namely the primitive Church, which was made up of Jews. For Christ too said: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]], that is, I was sent first and principally to the Synagogue. Therefore Paul said to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei]]. Then [[1:16|and to the Greek|et Græco]], that is, to those converted from heathendom, the Gospel avails. By the Greeks, as by the worthier part, he signifies the Gentiles. For when the preaching of the Apostles was rejected by the Jews, a just passing over to the Gentiles took place, as Paul testifies: [[Acts 13:46|because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold we turn to the Gentiles|Quia repulistis illud, et indignos vos judicastis vitæ æternæ, ecce convertimur ad gentes]]. According to Haymo, the Gospel is called the power of God because it proclaims Christ the power of God[[1 Cor 1:24||]]. According to Ambrose, it is called the power of God because it avails for the forgiveness of sins and for the working of miracles.

paras.t: Quod autem Evangelium sit virtus Dei, proficiens in salutem omni credenti, consequenter declarat. Justitia enim Dei in eo revelatur ex fide in fidem. Hæc justitia Dei, quæ revelatur seu manifestatur in Evangelio, sicut in scriptura veraci, vel in Judæo et Græco, sicut in subjecto justificato, tripliciter intelligi potest : Primo, de increata justitia Creatoris, quæ est ipsemet Deus sanctus et justus. In Evangelio quippe increata Dei Patris justitia declaratur sive describitur : quomodo scilicet maluit Unigenitum suum pati et mori, quam peccata manere inulta; et quomodo Christus per viam justitiæ mundum redemit; quomodo etiam Pater omne judicium præstitit Christo, et per ipsum judicaturus est omnes, daturusque singulis quod merentur. Nunc tamen potissimum loquitur sanctus Apostolus de justitia Dei qua infideles et impii justificati sunt gratis. — Sed quum hoc ad misericordiam Dei pertineat, mirum videtur quomodo illud justitiæ adscribatur. Et respondendum, secundum Anselmum, quod tanta est bonitas atque benignitas Dei, ut justum sit eum etiam indignis et impiis misereri ac parcere. Sicque, ut hujusmodi actu attenditur justitia ex parte bonitatis divinæ secundum se ipsam acceptæ, misericordia quoque in eo attenditur ex parte bonitatis divinæ ad indignos relatæ. Secundo exponitur de justitia Dei creata, quam ipse causat in nobis : per quam justificamur formaliter, quia per eam Deus justificat nos gratis, per fidem sine operibus legis. Dando enim animæ fidem et gratiam, confert justitiam, per quam anima justificatur. Hæc justitia in Evangelio revelatur, et in Christianorum cordibus manifestatur. — Tertio exponitur de fideli ac vera divinarum promissionum adimpletione, qua Deus in Ecclesia et in Evangelio adimplevit quod in veteri Testamento prædixit, atque in populo Synagogæ præsignavit. Hæc justitia in Evangelio revelatur, Christo testante : Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege et Prophetis et Psalmis de me; et alibi, Unum iota non peribit de lege, donec omnia fiant. De prædicta justitia Dei secundo modo accepta, alio loco dicit Apostolus, loquens de Judæis : Ignorantes Dei justitiam, et suam volentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti ; et rursus, Inveniar in illo, non habens meam justitiam quæ ex lege est, sed quæ ex fide. Unde per Prophetam Dominus ait : Prope est justitia mea ut reveletur. Erat namque in veteri lege velata, sed in Evangelio est revelata. De qua justitia dicit Salvator : Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit ; et alibi, Fides tua te salvam fecit ; itemque, Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam.
paras.en: That the Gospel is the power of God, availing unto salvation for every one who believes, he next shows: [[1:17|For the justice of God is revealed therein, from faith unto faith|Justitia enim Dei in eo revelatur ex fide in fidem]]. This justice of God, which is revealed or made manifest in the Gospel, as in a truthful writing, or in the Jew and the Greek, as in the subject justified, may be understood in three ways. First, of the uncreated justice of the Creator, which is God Himself, holy and just. For in the Gospel the uncreated justice of God the Father is declared or described: namely, how He chose that His Only-begotten should suffer and die rather than that sins should remain unpunished; and how Christ redeemed the world by the way of justice; how also the Father has given all judgment to Christ[[John 5:22||]], and through Him will judge all[[2 Tim 4:1||]], and give to each what he deserves. Yet here the holy Apostle speaks chiefly of the justice of God by which unbelievers and the ungodly are justified freely. — But since this belongs to the mercy of God, it seems strange how it is ascribed to justice. The answer, according to Anselm, is that so great is the goodness and kindness of God that it is just for Him to have mercy on and spare even the unworthy and the ungodly. And so, as justice is regarded in such an act on the side of the divine goodness taken in itself, mercy also is regarded in it on the side of the divine goodness as related to the unworthy. Secondly, it is expounded of the created justice of God, which He causes in us, by which we are formally justified, since by it God justifies us freely, through faith without the works of the law. For by giving the soul faith and grace He confers justice, by which the soul is justified. This justice is revealed in the Gospel and made manifest in the hearts of Christians. — Thirdly, it is expounded of the faithful and true fulfilment of the divine promises, by which God fulfilled in the Church and in the Gospel what He foretold in the Old Testament and prefigured in the people of the Synagogue. This justice is revealed in the Gospel, as Christ testifies: [[Luke 24:44|all things must needs be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses and in the prophets and in the psalms, concerning me|Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege et Prophetis et Psalmis de me]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 5:18|one jot, or one tittle shall not pass of the law, till all be fulfilled|Unum iota non peribit de lege, donec omnia fiant]]. Of the aforesaid justice of God taken in the second way the Apostle says in another place, speaking of the Jews: [[Rom 10:3|not knowing the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God|Ignorantes Dei justitiam, et suam volentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti]]; and again, [[Phil 3:9|may be found in him, not having my justice, which is of the law, but that which is of the faith|Inveniar in illo, non habens meam justitiam quæ ex lege est, sed quæ ex fide]]. Whence the Lord says by the Prophet: My justice is near, to be revealed [the margin gives Is. xlvi, 13; Denis's wording is closer to Is 56:1]. For it was veiled in the old law, but in the Gospel it is revealed. Of which justice the Saviour says: [[Mark 16:16|He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved|Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 9:22|thy faith hath made thee whole|Fides tua te salvam fecit]]; and again, [[John 6:47|He that believeth in me hath everlasting life|Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam]].

paras.t: Quælibet justitia Dei nunc prædicta, revelatur ex fide in fidem, hoc est, ex fide Prophetarum et Patriarcharum, in fidem Apostolorum atque Ecclesiæ : quia quod illi crediderunt futurum, isti crediderunt impletum. Vel, Ex fide, id est ex actu fidei unius articuli, in fidem, hoc est in actum fidei alterius articuli. Omnia namque testimonia fidei sunt connexa, et unum ex alio magis credibile redditur, imo et quodammodo declaratur, magisque planum ac rationale judicatur. Sicut scriptum est : Justus autem ex fide vivit. Hoc allegat Apostolus ad probandum, quod justitia Dei revelatur in Evangelio, vel in Christiano, ex fide in fidem.
paras.en: Each justice of God just mentioned is revealed [[1:17|from faith unto faith|ex fide in fidem]], that is, from the faith of the Prophets and Patriarchs into the faith of the Apostles and of the Church: because what those believed as to come, these believed as fulfilled. Or, *from faith*, that is, from the act of faith in one article, *unto faith*, that is, into the act of faith in another article.
