Hence it is written in the Canonical Epistle of John: [[1 John 3:1|Behold what manner of charity the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called and should be|Videte qualem caritatem dedit nobis Deus Pater, ut filii Dei nominemur et simus]]. Now as almighty God moves the other creatures to their proper operations and natural end by a certain universal influence or general government (as Proclus, the author of the book *On Causes*, affirms: The first cause rules all things without being mingled with them), so He moves the rational creature to its supernatural end by a special government and inspiration, which is called providence. And the elect He moves and rules singularly, providing them not only sufficiently but also efficaciously with all things necessary to salvation, so that they receive God's grace and yield to His inspiration. Therefore they are said rather to be *driven* [Latin *agi*, rendered “led” in the Douay] than ruled or moved by the Holy Ghost, to suggest the greatness of grace. For a meritorious act requires not only habitual grace, but also a certain actual motion of the Holy Ghost stirring the will. Wherefore the Prophet said: [[Is 26:12|Lord, thou wilt give us peace: for thou hast wrought all our works for us|Domine … omnia … opera nostra operatus es nobis]]. — Further, since this motion or influence, action and prompting of the Holy Ghost is wholly supernatural, the soul needs certain supernatural habits by which it is fitted and disposed to receive this motion readily. These habits are the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]], which are habitual and supernatural dispositions infused by God immediately by creation, whereby the soul is made readily movable by the Holy Ghost towards its supernatural end, which is life everlasting. These gifts are really distinct from the virtues and excel them in dignity, the theological virtues excepted. By these gifts the soul is directed by the Holy Ghost, so that it hears Him as a master. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 142:10|Thy good spirit shall lead me into the right land|Spiritus tuus bonus deducet me in terram rectam]]. — Those, then, who are thus led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God. And whoever is in grace has these gifts in some degree, and is led by the Holy Ghost as far as the state of salvation requires, namely to the keeping of the commandments.

paras.t: Deinde ponitur ratio cur morituri simus, si secundum carnem vixerimus. Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, id est, jam tempore gratiæ, non est vobis datus spiritus quo serviatis Deo serviliter quasi invite, videlicet timore pœnarum, ut olim tempore legis, quæ comminatione pœnarum induxit homines ad serviendum ; sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum Dei, id est spiritum cujus gratia homines adoptantur in filios Dei, in quo clamamus ore vel corde : Abba (Pater). Duo sunt nomina, unum Hebraeum, alterum Latinum, significantia idem. Et est sensus : In hoc spiritu vocamus ex caritate, tanquam filii adoptivi, Deum Patrem fiducialiter atque affectuose, dicentes : Pater noster qui es in cœlis.
paras.en: Next is given the reason why we shall die if we live according to the flesh. [[8:15|For you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear|Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore]], that is, now in the time of grace there has not been given you a spirit by which you serve God servilely, as it were unwillingly, namely through fear of punishment, as formerly in the time of the law, which by threat of punishment brought men to serve[[Deut 28:15||]]; [[8:15|but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons|sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum]] of God, that is, the spirit by whose grace men are adopted as sons of God, [[8:15|whereby we cry|in quo clamamus]] with mouth or heart: [[8:15|Abba (Father)|Abba (Pater)]]. These are two names, one Hebrew, the other Latin, meaning the same. And the sense is: In this spirit we call upon God the Father out of charity, as adopted sons, confidently and lovingly, saying: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]].

paras.t: Glossa per spiritum servitutis, intelligit Spiritum Sanctum, a quo cordibus Judæorum incussus est timor pœnarum, quo serviliter servierunt. Nam et timor servilis, in quantum est timor, a Spiritu Sancto est. Sic enim retrahit a peccato et disponit ad gratiam. Quantum vero ad servilitatem suam, nec bonus est, neque a Spiritu Sancto. Dicitur ergo Spiritus Sanctus, spiritus servitutis, ratione sui effectus, quia facit servire. Quantum ad hoc, receperunt [eum] qui ejus dono gratis dato servierunt timore pœnarum. Per spiritum vero adoptionis, intelligit Glossa eumdem Spiritum Sanctum per gratiam adoptantem. Unde Augustinus : Cave, inquit, ne ex eo quod ait, Spiritum servitutis, et, Spiritum adoptionis, diversum intelligas spiritum, quum sit unus atque idem Spiritus, qui in Trinitate dicitur Spiritus Sanctus : quod etiam Apostolus ostendit, dicens, Iterum. Sed propter diversa opera dissimiliter nominatur. Huic dicto concordat quod de Spiritu subditur, Ipse enim Spiritus testimonium reddit spiritui nostro, quod sumus filii Dei : quod certum est dici de Spiritu Sancto, videturque dictum de eodem spiritu de quo nunc agitur.
paras.en: The Gloss understands by the spirit of bondage the Holy Ghost, by whom the fear of punishment was struck into the hearts of the Jews, through which they served servilely. For servile fear too, insofar as it is fear, is from the Holy Ghost; for thus it draws back from sin and disposes to grace. But as to its servility, it is neither good nor from the Holy Ghost. The Holy Ghost, then, is called the spirit of bondage by reason of His effect, because He makes men serve. In this respect they received Him who, by His gift freely given [*gratis datum*, a grace given for others' good or without sanctifying], served through fear of punishment. By the spirit of adoption the Gloss understands the same Holy Ghost adopting through grace. Hence Augustine says: Beware lest, from his saying “the spirit of bondage” and “the spirit of adoption”, you understand a different spirit, since it is one and the same Spirit who in the Trinity is called the Holy Ghost: which the Apostle also shows by saying “again”. But because of different works He is named differently. With this agrees what is added of the Spirit: [[8:16|For the Spirit himself giveth testimony to our spirit that we are the sons of God|Ipse enim Spiritus testimonium reddit spiritui nostro, quod sumus filii Dei]]: which is certainly said of the Holy Ghost, and seems said of the same spirit now treated.

paras.t: Quidam vero per spiritum intelligunt donum Spiritus Sancti : ut spiritus adoptionis dicatur donum filialis timoris, qui nos efficit filios Dei; spiritus vero servitutis intelligatur donum timoris servilis, videlicet ipse timor servilis. Hæc enim, secundum Augustinum, est brevis differentia legis et Evangelii : timor et amor. Lex vetus appellata est lex timoris, quoniam comminatione pœnarum induxit ad bonum, nec præstitit gratiam obediendi per caritatem. Porro lex evangelica, est lex amoris : agit enim, gratiam conferendo, servire Deo amore justitiæ. Non est autem sic intelligendum, quin multi in veteri Testamento acceperunt spiritum adoptionis filiorum Dei. Omnes enim electi habuerunt hunc spiritum, sed non ex lege, neque per legem, magis autem ex Deo per fidem qua crediderunt in Christum venturum, ad cujus gratiam confugerunt, legis insufficientiam cognoscentes, propriamque infirmitatem pensantes.
paras.en: Some, however, understand by spirit a gift of the Holy Ghost: so that the spirit of adoption is the gift of filial fear, which makes us sons of God, and the spirit of bondage is the gift of servile fear, namely servile fear itself. For this, according to Augustine, is the brief difference between the Law and the Gospel: fear and love. The old law was called the law of fear because it led to good by threat of punishment and did not give the grace of obeying through charity. But the Gospel law is the law of love: for by conferring grace it makes men serve God out of love of justice. Yet this is not to be understood as though many in the Old Testament did not receive the spirit of adoption of the sons of God. For all the elect had this spirit, but not from the law nor through the law, but rather from God, through the faith by which they believed in Christ to come, to whose grace they fled, knowing the insufficiency of the law and weighing their own weakness.

paras.t: Videtur quoque per spiritum hoc loco posse intelligi spiritus rationalis creatus, videlicet anima nostra. Quamvis autem quilibet nostrum acceperit hunc spiritum suum, quando creata corporique infusa est anima sua, dicimur tamen spiritum istum recipere vel amittere, quando aliqua nova dispositio ei confertur vel aufertur, quemadmodum aliquis dicitur concipere spiritum devotum, vel perdere animam ferventem. Juxta quem sensum Dominus ait : Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, et dabo vobis cor carneum. Qui ergo sub lege servierunt timore, accepisse dicuntur spiritum servitutis, id est animam servientem in timore. Qui vero sub gratia serviunt caritate, accipiunt spiritum adoptionis, id est animam habentem gratiam adoptionis : in quo spiritu clamant corde devoto, Abba (Pater). Huic vero consonat quod alibi ait Apostolus : Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis.
paras.en: It seems too that by spirit in this place may be understood the created rational spirit, namely our soul. Although each of us received this his spirit when his soul was created and infused into the body, we are yet said to receive or lose this spirit when some new disposition is conferred on it or taken from it, as one is said to conceive a devout spirit or to lose a fervent soul. In which sense the Lord says: [[Ezech 36:26|I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and will give you a heart of flesh|Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, et dabo vobis cor carneum]]. Those, then, who under the law served in fear are said to have received the spirit of bondage, that is, a soul serving in fear. But those who under grace serve in charity receive the spirit of adoption, that is, a soul having the grace of adoption: in which spirit they cry with devout heart, Abba (Father). With this agrees what the Apostle says elsewhere: [[2 Tim 1:7|For God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power and of love|Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis]].

paras.t: Quod autem in Spiritu Sancto clamemus, Abba (Pater), et Deum vere Patrem vocemus, hinc constat : Ipse enim Spiritus Sanctus testimonium reddit spiritui nostro, id est, testificatur animæ nostræ, eamque recognoscere facit per inspirationem internam, vel revelationem apertam, quod sumus filii Dei adoptivi, stando in caritate et gratia.
paras.en: That we cry in the Holy Ghost, Abba (Father), and truly call God Father, is clear from this: [[8:16|For the Spirit himself giveth testimony to our spirit|Ipse enim Spiritus Sanctus testimonium reddit spiritui nostro]] (the Holy Ghost), that is, testifies to our soul and makes it recognize, by inward inspiration or open revelation, [[8:16|that we are the sons of God|quod sumus filii Dei]] by adoption, while we stand in charity and grace.

paras.t: Testificatio ista multis modis intelligi potest. Primo, per manifestam et claram revelationem Spiritus Sancti, sive fiat immediate ab ipso, sive per angelum : sicque agnoscit homo per certitudinem se esse in gratia et filiatione divina, sicut Paulus et ceteri Apostoli, imo et multi perfecti ita sciverunt se esse in gratia. Ad quos maxime pertinet quod alio loco dicit Apostolus : Nos non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. Hoc modo agnovit Abraham se esse filium Dei, quum ei Dominus promisit quod decederet in senectute bona. Ezechias quoque certissime dixit : Memento, Domine, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et in corde perfecto. Secundo, fit testificatio ista per quamdam bonæ fiduciæ consolatoriam infusionem : ut quum homo nimium anxiatur an placeat Deo, et subito sentit se consolari et quasi certificari. Sic autem omnes virtuosi et boni scire possunt se esse filios Dei, non quidem certo, sed conjecturaliter et probabiliter. Tertio, fit per propriæ conversationis et conscientiæ diligentem discussionem : ut quum homo non habet remorsum mortalis peccati, et cum debita diligentia custodit mandata, auditque verbum Dei libenter. Ista sunt probabilia signa filiationis divinæ, imo et prædestinationis, secundum quod ait Salvator : Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit; et Joannes in sua Canonica, Si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum ; et rursus, Qui servat verbum Christi, vere in hoc caritas Dei perfecta est. — Denique, sicut vita naturæ cognoscitur ex vitalibus actibus ac naturalibus motibus animæ, sic vita gratiæ ex bonis operibus, seu mandatorum custodia comprobatur, quia ut Gregorius ait, Exhibitio operis, probatio est caritatis. Quum ergo Spiritus Sanctus facit nos bene agere, atque in Dei obsequio promptos et agiles esse, tunc utique testimonium perhibet spiritui nostro, quod filii Dei simus.
paras.en: This testimony can be understood in many ways. First, by a manifest and clear revelation of the Holy Ghost, whether made immediately by Him or through an angel: and so a man knows with certainty that he is in grace and divine sonship, as Paul and the other Apostles, and indeed many perfect souls, thus knew themselves to be in grace. To these chiefly belongs what the Apostle says in another place: [[1 Cor 2:12|Now, we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Nos non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]. In this way Abraham knew himself to be a son of God, when the Lord promised him that he should die in a good old age[[Gen 15:15||]]. Ezechias also most certainly said: [[4 Kings 20:3|remember how I have walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart|Memento, Domine, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et in corde perfecto]]. Secondly, this testimony is given by a consoling infusion of good confidence: as when a man is greatly anxious whether he pleases God, and suddenly feels himself consoled and as it were assured. In this way all virtuous and good men can know that they are sons of God, not indeed with certainty, but by conjecture and probably. Thirdly, it is given through diligent examination of one's own conduct and conscience: as when a man has no remorse of mortal sin, keeps the commandments with due diligence, and gladly hears the word of God. These are probable signs of divine sonship, and even of predestination, as the Saviour says: [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]]; and John in his Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:21|if our heart do not reprehend us, we have confidence towards God|Si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum]]; and again: [[1 John 2:5|But he that keepeth his word, in him in very deed the charity of God is perfected|Qui servat verbum Christi, vere in hoc caritas Dei perfecta est]]. — Lastly, as the life of nature is known from the vital acts and natural movements of the soul, so the life of grace is proved by good works, or the keeping of the commandments; for, as Gregory says, the showing of the work is the proof of love. When therefore the Holy Ghost makes us act well and be prompt and nimble in God's service, then indeed He bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God.

paras.t: Huic ergo dicto Apostoli non repugnat quod scriptum est : Sunt justi atque sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt ; et tamen nescit homo utrum amore an odio dignus sit, sed omnia in futurum servantur incerta. Et quod ait beatus Job : Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum, et si recesserit a me, non intelligam ; itemque, Si simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea. Hæc enim atque similia ideo asseruntur, quia de lege communi et humano processu seu via, non potest homo agnoscere per certitudinem se esse filium Dei per gratiæ adoptionem. Postremo, melius atque facilius potest quis scire se esse in gratia et esse filium Dei secundum præsentem justitiam, quam esse prædestinatum, vel in gratia permansurum. Unde hoc certo agnosci non potest, nisi per revelationem divinam.
paras.en: This saying of the Apostle, then, is not contradicted by what is written: [[Eccles 9:1|there are just men and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God|Sunt justi atque sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt]]: and yet [[Eccles 9:1|man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|nescit homo utrum amore an odio dignus sit]], [[Eccles 9:2|But all things are kept uncertain|sed omnia in futurum servantur incerta]]. Nor by what blessed Job says: [[Job 9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him: if he depart, I shall not understand|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum, et si recesserit a me, non intelligam]]; and likewise: [[Job 9:21|Although I should be simple, even this my soul shall be ignorant of|Si simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]]. For these and like things are asserted because by the common law and the human course or way a man cannot know with certainty that he is a son of God by the adoption of grace. Finally, one can know better and more easily that he is in grace and a son of God according to present justice than that he is predestined or will persevere in grace. This latter cannot be known with certainty except by divine revelation.

paras.t: Si autem filii Dei jam sumus per gratiam adoptantem, et heredes erimus in patria per gloriam beatificantem. Filiis enim adoptivis debetur aliqua pars hereditatis paternæ. Erimus autem heredes quidem, non cujuscumque, sed Dei, æternaliter possidendo bona Domini in terra viventium, quæ oculus non vidit nec auris audivit. Maxime tamen ista Beatorum hereditas est ipsa Divinitas, quæ est objectalis beatitudo indivisibilis in se : quæ tota habetur a singulis, a nullo autem totaliter, et ita dividitur secundum quod diversimode participatur : quæ diversitas est ex parte recipientium, quorum unus alio clarius conspicit Deum. De hac hereditate fertur in Psalmo : Dominus pars hereditatis meæ ; et, Satiabor quum apparuerit gloria tua. Per Isaiam quoque Dominus loquitur : Sustollam te super altitudinem terræ, et cibabo te hereditate patris tui Jacob. Ceteræ hereditates terminantur in morte. Hæc autem a morte sumit exordium, juxta illud : Quum dederit dilectis suis somnum, ecce hereditas Domini. Coheredes autem Christi, id est, beatitudinis Christi consortes atque participes erimus. Ipse est enim principalis heres, et nos simul cum ipso divinam beatitudinem consequemur. Quo autem merito, subditur : si tamen compatimur, id est, Christi passionibus configuremur, bajulando crucem nostram, et sequendo vestigia ejus : ad hunc finem, ut et simul glorificemur, id est, gloriosi efficiamur cum Christo glorificato, quemadmodum ipse profitetur : Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, et illi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam.
paras.en: [[8:17|And if sons|Si autem filii]] of God we now are by adopting grace, [[8:17|heirs also|et hæredes]] we shall be in the fatherland by beatifying glory. For to adopted sons some part of the father's inheritance is due. And we shall be [[8:17|heirs indeed of God|hæredes, quidem Dei]], not of anyone at all, but of God, possessing eternally the good things of the Lord in the land of the living[[Ps 26:13||]], which [[1 Cor 2:9|Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard|oculus non vidit nec auris audivit]]. But above all this inheritance of the Blessed is the Godhead itself, which is the objective beatitude, indivisible in itself: which is had wholly by each, but by none totally [that is, each possesses the whole God, but none comprehends Him fully], and so is divided according as it is shared in diverse ways; which diversity is on the part of the receivers, one of whom sees God more clearly than another. Of this inheritance it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 15:5|The Lord is the portion of my inheritance|Dominus pars hereditatis meæ]]; and: [[Ps 16:15|I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear|Satiabor quum apparuerit gloria tua]]. Through Isaias also the Lord says: [[Is 58:14|I will lift thee up above the high places of the earth, and will feed thee with the inheritance of Jacob thy father|Sustollam te super altitudinem terræ, et cibabo te hereditate patris tui Jacob]] [the margin gives Is. lviii, 14]. Other inheritances end at death; but this one takes its beginning from death, according to that: [[Ps 126:2|When he shall give sleep|Quum dederit dilectis suis somnum]], [[Ps 126:3|Behold the inheritance of the Lord|ecce hereditas Domini]]. [[8:17|and joint heirs with Christ|cohæredes autem Christi]], that is, we shall be sharers and partakers of Christ's beatitude. For He is the principal heir, and we together with Him shall attain the divine beatitude. And by what merit is added: [[8:17|if we suffer with him|si tamen compatimur]], that is, if we are conformed to the sufferings of Christ, carrying our cross[[Matt 16:24||]][[Luke 14:27||]] and following in His footsteps: to this end, [[8:17|that we may be also glorified with him|ut et conglorificemur]] [Denis divides it, *simul glorificemur*], that is, be made glorious with Christ glorified, as He Himself declares: [[John 17:24|Father, I will that where I am, they also whom thou hast given me may be with me: that they may see my glory|Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, et illi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam]].

8.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS HUJUS CAPITULI OCTAVI, AB EO LOCO QUO DICITUR : EXISTIMO ENIM QUOD NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, ETC.
8.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this eighth chapter, from the place where it is said: For I reckon that the sufferings are not worthy, etc.

paras.t: HORTATUR nos insuper sanctus Apostolus, ut Christo compatiamur, quatenus conglorificemur, eo quod præmium incomparabiliter majus sit merito. Existimo enim, id est, agnosco ego, qui de talibus veraciter judico. Dicit autem, Existimo, non quasi incertus aut dubitans, sed sobrium modum loquendi servans, ac edocens ne immoderati simus in asserendo. Quod non sunt condignæ, id est æquales, sufficientes ac proportionatæ, secundum rigorem justitiæ, passiones, id est persecutiones, tentationes, labores, hujus temporis, id est, quas in hoc brevi vitæ hujus curriculo sustinemus, ad futuram gloriam, scilicet vitam æternam promerendam, quæ revelabitur in nobis, id est, clare et coram omnibus nobis prædestinatis præstabitur. Unde Salvator : Quum feceritis, ait, omnia quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite : Servi inutiles sumus. Hæc enim gloria, est beatifica visio divinæ essentiæ, plena mentis in Deo lætitia, status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus, consummata animæ et corporis glorificatio sempiterna : ad quam promerendam, temporales passiones condignæ non sunt. — Sed videtur contrarium, quia secundum doctores, homo in caritate stans, meretur de condigno vitam æternam. Et respondendum, quod passiones seu opera caritatis considerantur dupliciter : Primo, secundum quod procedunt a libero arbitrio, vel acceptantur ab eo : sicque non merentur vitam æternam de condigno, etiam habitu caritatis adjuncto. Secundo, prout Spiritus Sanctus liberum arbitrium movens, est hujus processionis vel acceptationis principium : et ita est meritum de condigno, eo quod principium meriti ejusdem rationis exsistat cum præmio. Apostolus vero loquitur de passionibus primo modo.
paras.en: The holy Apostle further exhorts us to suffer with Christ, so that we may be glorified with Him, because the reward is incomparably greater than the merit. [[8:18|For I reckon|Existimo enim]], that is, I acknowledge, I who judge truly of such things. He says *I reckon*, not as one uncertain or doubting, but keeping a sober manner of speech, and teaching us not to be immoderate in asserting. [[8:18|are not worthy to be compared|Quod non sunt condignæ]], that is, equal, sufficient and proportioned according to the rigour of justice, [[8:18|the sufferings|passiones]], that is, persecutions, temptations, labours, [[8:18|of this time|hujus temporis]], that is, which we bear in this brief course of this life, [[8:18|with the glory to come|ad futuram gloriam]], namely for meriting eternal life, [[8:18|that shall be revealed in us|quæ revelabitur in nobis]], that is, which shall be bestowed clearly and openly upon all of us who are predestined. Hence the Saviour says: [[Luke 17:10|when you shall have done all these things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants|feceritis, ait, omnia quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite : Servi inutiles sumus]]. For this glory is the beatific vision of the divine essence, the full joy of the mind in God, a state made perfect by the gathering of all goods, the consummate and everlasting glorification of soul and body: for meriting which temporal sufferings are not worthy. — But the contrary seems true, since according to the doctors a man standing in charity merits eternal life *de condigno* [that is, by a merit strictly proportioned to the reward, as distinct from merit *de congruo*, of fittingness]. The answer is that sufferings or works of charity are considered in two ways. First, as they proceed from free will or are accepted by it: and so they do not merit eternal life *de condigno*, even with the habit of charity added. Second, inasmuch as the Holy Ghost, moving free will, is the principle of this proceeding or accepting: and thus there is merit *de condigno*, because the principle of the merit is of the same order as the reward. The Apostle speaks of sufferings in the first way.

paras.t: Quod autem gloria ista nobis præstanda sit, probat. Nam exspectatio creaturæ, id est creatura exspectans, videlicet homo viator. Dicitur enim homo omnis creatura, juxta illud, Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ : primo, propter communionem, quia cum omni genere creaturarum in aliquo convenit; secundo, propter excellentiam, quoniam omnia corporalia propter ipsum creata sunt. Revelationem filiorum Dei exspectat, id est, manifestationem beatitudinis electorum in patria, scilicet sui ipsius felicitatem et glorificationem, cum ingenti desiderio præstolatur, dicens quotidie : Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus. Nunc quippe filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quid erimus. Scimus quoniam quum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Nunc ergo exspectamus hanc apparitionem, quatenus mente et corpore glorificati, declaremur seu agnoscamur esse filii Dei per similitudinem gloriæ.
paras.en: That this glory is to be bestowed on us he proves. [[8:19|For the expectation of the creature|Nam exspectatio creaturæ]], that is, the creature that waits, namely man the wayfarer. For man is called every creature, according to that saying, [[Mark 16:15|preach the gospel to every creature|Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]: first, by reason of communion, because he agrees in something with every kind of creature; second, by reason of excellence, since all bodily things were created for his sake[[Gen 1:26||]]. [[8:19|waiteth for the revelation of the sons of God|Revelationem filiorum Dei exspectat]], that is, it awaits with immense desire the manifestation of the beatitude of the elect in the fatherland, namely its own happiness and glorification, saying daily: [[Ps 41:2|As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God|Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus]]. For [[1 John 3:2|we are now the sons of God: and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he shall appear we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is|Nunc quippe filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quid erimus. Scimus quoniam quum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est]]. Now therefore we await this appearing, so that, glorified in mind and body, we may be declared or acknowledged to be sons of God by the likeness of glory.

paras.t: Vanitati enim, id est instabilitati, mortalitati, multisque pœnis, creatura subjecta est, id est homo, quemadmodum ait Scriptura : Verumtamen universa vanitas, omnis homo vivens; non volens, id est non sponte, quia invitus hæc patitur; vel, Non volens, id est propter originale peccatum, quod non est nostra voluntate commissum, cujus pœnas cogimur tolerare ; sed propter eum qui subjecit eam in spe, id est, propter divinam justitiam subjectus est homo vanitati huic, clementer tamen, quia in spe liberationis futuræ. Quia et ipsa creatura, videlicet homo, liberabitur, in futura resurrectione, a servitute corruptionis, id est corruptione ista servili et corporali, vel magis proprie a servitute corruptionis, id est sollicitudinibus vitæ præsentis, videlicet a cura quærendi vestitum et victum, ac alia quibus hæc corruptibilis vita sustentatur, eique servitur. Liberabitur autem, pertingendo in libertatem gloriæ, id est in dominium et securitatem felicitatis, vel in gloriosam libertatem filiorum Dei, id est electorum seu Beatorum in patria, qui Deo perfecte assimilantur, et plena dilectione incessabiliter conjunguntur. Hæc autem consequenter declarat Apostolus.
paras.en: [[8:20|For the creature was made subject to vanity|Vanitati enim creatura subjecta est]]: *vanity*, that is, instability, mortality and many pains; *the creature*, that is, man, as Scripture says: [[Ps 38:6|all things are vanity: every man living|universa vanitas, omnis homo vivens]]; [[8:20|not willingly|non volens]], that is, not of its own accord, because it suffers these things unwillingly; or, *not willingly*, that is, on account of original sin, which was not committed by our own will, and whose penalties we are forced to bear; [[8:20|but by reason of him that made it subject, in hope|sed propter eum qui subjecit eam in spe]], that is, on account of divine justice man was made subject to this vanity, yet mercifully, because in hope of future deliverance. [[8:21|Because the creature also itself|Quia et ipsa creatura]], namely man, [[8:21|shall be delivered|liberabitur]] in the future resurrection [[8:21|from the servitude of corruption|a servitute corruptionis]], that is, from this servile and bodily corruption; or more properly, *from the servitude of corruption*, that is, from the cares of the present life, namely from the care of seeking clothing and food and the other things by which this corruptible life is sustained and served. And it shall be delivered by attaining [[8:21|into the liberty of the glory|in libertatem gloriæ]], that is, into the dominion and security of happiness, or into the glorious liberty [[8:21|of the children of God|filiorum Dei]], that is, of the elect or the Blessed in the fatherland, who are perfectly likened to God and unceasingly joined to Him in full love. These things the Apostle next explains.

paras.t: Scimus enim quod omnis creatura ingemiscit et parturit usque adhuc. Hoc duobus modis exponitur. Primo, de omni homine mortali : qui dicitur ingemiscere, suspirando ad patriam, et propter vitæ hujus angustias frequenter gemens et flens in hac valle lacrimarum; et parturire, id est cum dolore operari; usque adhuc, quia a principio mundi usque in præsens tempus ita fecit, et usque ad mortem finemque sæculi durabit gemitus iste et parturitio. Secundo exponitur generaliter de principalibus partibus hujus mundi sensibilis, scilicet elementis atque cœlestibus orbibus : quæ dicuntur ingemiscere et parturire metaphorice, sicut campus dicitur exsultare, et pratum ridere. Unde per gemitum eorum, intelligitur inclinatio vel appetitus eorum ad statum perfectiorem; per parturitionem autem, mutua generatio et corruptio quantum ad elementa, vel continua circumvolutio quantum ad cœlestia corpora. Ex quibus elicitur, quod secundum intentionem Apostoli, corpora cœlestia et elementa in fine sæculi, glorificatis electis judicioque peracto, innovabuntur, ita quod elementorum transmutatio et cœlestium corporum motus cessabunt, ampliori quoque lumine vestientur. Terra enim, ut fertur, in superficie lucida erit ut vitrum, aqua sicut crystallus, aer ut cœlum, ignis ut stellæ. Quantitas autem meliorationis cœlestium corporum nota est ei qui daturus est eam. Verumtamen de mensura decorationis solis et lunæ scriptum est : Erit lux lunæ sicut lux solis, et lux solis septempliciter sicut lux septem dierum. Tunc enim tanta erit lux lunæ, quanta nunc est lux solis; corpora quoque Beatorum septies clariora erunt, ut dicitur, sole. Hoc tamen secundum B. Thomam, nec ratione nec auctoritate probatur, quamvis certissime verum esse sciamus quod veritas ait : Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum.
paras.en: [[8:22|For we know that every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now|Scimus enim quod omnis creatura ingemiscit et parturit usque adhuc]]. This is expounded in two ways. First, of every mortal man: who is said to *groan* by sighing for the fatherland, and, because of the straits of this life, often groaning and weeping in this vale of tears; and to *travail*, that is, to work with pain; *even till now*, because from the beginning of the world until the present time he has done so, and this groaning and travail will last until death and the end of the world. Second, it is expounded generally of the principal parts of this sensible world, namely the elements and the heavenly spheres: which are said to groan and travail metaphorically, as a field is said to rejoice[[Ps 95:12||]] and a meadow to smile. So by their groaning is understood their inclination or appetite toward a more perfect state; by their travail, the mutual generation and corruption as regards the elements, or the continual revolution as regards the heavenly bodies. From which it is drawn that, according to the Apostle's intent, the heavenly bodies and the elements will be renewed at the end of the world, when the elect have been glorified and the judgement completed, so that the transmutation of the elements and the motion of the heavenly bodies will cease, and they will be clothed with greater light. For the earth, as is said, will be bright on its surface like glass, the water like crystal, the air like the sky, the fire like the stars. The amount of the bettering of the heavenly bodies is known to Him who is to give it. Yet of the measure of the adornment of sun and moon it is written: [[Is 30:26|the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days|Erit lux lunæ sicut lux solis, et lux solis septempliciter sicut lux septem dierum]]. For then the light of the moon will be as great as the light of the sun is now; and the bodies of the Blessed will be, as is said, seven times brighter than the sun. This, however, according to blessed Thomas, is proved neither by reason nor by authority, although we know most surely to be true what the Truth says: [[Matt 13:43|shall the just shine as the sun, in the kingdom of their Father|Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum]].

paras.t: Mihi præterea, semper salvo meliori judicio, videtur, quod sicut præsens locus quo dicitur, Scimus quod omnis creatura ingemiscit et parturit, exponitur de prædictis corporibus, sic superiora ab eo loco quo dictum est, Nam exspectatio creaturæ, de eisdem possint exponi : præsertim quum Apostolus, dicendo, Exspectatio creaturæ revelationem filiorum Dei exspectat, et ipsa creatura liberabitur a servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei, manifeste videatur distinguere inter creaturam, et filios Dei adoptionis de quibus prædixit, scilicet homines prædestinatos. Erit igitur sensus : Exspectatio creaturæ elementalis atque cœlestis, revelationem filiorum Dei, id est manifestam glorificationem hominum electorum, exspectat, secundum quod ex divina ordinatione inclinatur ad quamdam clarificationem, quam in fine sæculi sortitura est, filiis Dei revelatis. Non enim innovabuntur corpora elementaria atque cœlestia, nisi corporibus electorum glorificatis, vel simul cum illis. Merito autem exspectat : Vanitati enim, id est mutabilitati vel transmutationi, creatura prædicta subjecta est, non volens, id est non ex se ipsa aut propria inclinatione, loquendo de ea prout ordinata est a Deo ad statum perfectum parificandum statui electorum post finale judicium, sed propter eum qui subjecit eam in spe, id est, ex ordinatione divina subjecta est huic vanitati propter hominem, ut ei deserviat. Corpora enim cœlestia propter generationem inferiorum, maxime hominum, moventur, et in generationibus mixtorum elementa concurrunt. Hæc autem subjectio facta est in spe præmemoratæ meliorationis seu clarificationis elementalium atque cœlestium, quia et ipsa creatura cœlestis et elementalis liberabitur a servitute corruptionis, id est a statu suæ variabilitatis, et a transmutatione ac motu, quibus corruptibilibus istis deservit.
paras.en: Moreover it seems to me, always saving a better judgement, that just as the present place, where it is said, *We know that every creature groaneth and travaileth*, is expounded of the aforesaid bodies, so the earlier verses, from the place where it was said, *For the expectation of the creature*, may be expounded of the same: especially since the Apostle, in saying, *The expectation of the creature waiteth for the revelation of the sons of God*, and *the creature itself shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God*, clearly seems to distinguish between the creature and the adopted sons of God of whom he spoke before, namely predestined men. The sense, then, will be: [[8:19|the expectation of the creature|Exspectatio creaturæ]], elemental and heavenly, [[8:19|waiteth for the revelation of the sons of God|revelationem filiorum Dei exspectat]], that is, the manifest glorification of elect men, inasmuch as by divine ordinance it is inclined toward a certain brightening, which it will receive at the end of the world, when the sons of God have been revealed. For the elemental and heavenly bodies will not be renewed except when the bodies of the elect have been glorified, or together with them. And rightly does it wait: [[8:20|For the creature was made subject to vanity|Vanitati enim creatura subjecta est]], *vanity*, that is, mutability or transmutation; *the creature* aforesaid; [[8:20|not willingly|non volens]], that is, not of itself or by its own inclination, speaking of it as ordained by God to a perfect state matching the state of the elect after the final judgement; [[8:20|but by reason of him that made it subject, in hope|sed propter eum qui subjecit eam in spe]], that is, by divine ordinance it was made subject to this vanity for man's sake, to serve him. For the heavenly bodies are moved for the generation of lower things, above all of men, and the elements concur in the generation of mixed bodies. And this subjection was made in hope of the aforementioned bettering or brightening of the elemental and heavenly things, [[8:21|Because the creature also itself|quia et ipsa creatura]], heavenly and elemental, [[8:21|shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption|liberabitur a servitute corruptionis]], that is, from its state of variability, and from the transmutation and motion by which it serves these corruptible things.

paras.t: Deinde ait Apostolus : Non solum autem illa, id est, non tantum omnis prædicta creatura ingemiscit ac parturit, sed et nos ipsi Apostoli Christi, quibus hoc minus convenire videtur, primitias Spiritus habentes, id est, abundantiorem gratiam Spiritus Sancti sortiti ; et ipsi intra nos gemimus cordialiter, suspirantes supernam Jerusalem, cupientes dissolvi, atque a præsentis vitæ ærumnis transferri, adoptionem filiorum Dei, id est consummatam adoptionem seu plenam adoptionis filiationem, videlicet præmium electorum in patria, exspectantes, non solum animæ glorificationem, sed et redemptionem corporis nostri, id est liberationem corporis nostri a mortalitate, pœnis atque miseriis, quibus modo vehementer affligitur. Propter quod David ait : Sitivit in te anima mea ; quam multipliciter tibi caro mea!
paras.en: Then the Apostle says: [[8:23|And not only it|Non solum autem illa]], that is, not only does every aforesaid creature groan and travail, [[8:23|but ourselves also|sed et nos ipsi]], the Apostles of Christ, whom this seems less to befit, [[8:23|who have the firstfruits of the Spirit|primitias Spiritus habentes]], that is, having received a more abundant grace of the Holy Ghost; [[8:23|even we ourselves groan within ourselves|et ipsi intra nos gemimus]] from the heart, sighing for the heavenly Jerusalem[[Ps 125:1||]], desiring to be dissolved[[Phil 1:23||]] and to be carried away from the miseries of the present life, [[8:23|waiting for the adoption of the sons of God|adoptionem filiorum Dei exspectantes]]: *the adoption*, that is, the consummated adoption or the full sonship of adoption, namely the reward of the elect in the fatherland; waiting not only for the glorification of the soul but also for [[8:23|the redemption of our body|redemptionem corporis nostri]], that is, the deliverance of our body from mortality, pains and miseries, by which it is now grievously afflicted. For which reason David says: [[Ps 62:2|For thee my soul hath thirsted; for thee my flesh, O how many ways!|Sitivit in te anima mea ; quam multipliciter tibi caro mea!]]!

paras.t: Præterea non inaniter hanc beatitudinem exspectamus. Spe enim salvi facti sumus, id est, actu spei tanquam merito liberati sumus a culpa, et digni effecti gloria. Actus namque virtutis salvat hoc modo. Vel sic : Spe salvi facti sumus, id est, per passionem ac meritum Christi jam beati et salvi sumus in spe, quamvis nondum beati sumus in re. Idcirco certissime præstolamur felicitatem prædictam. Spes autem, id est res sperata, quæ videtur, id est, jam præsens atque obtenta est, non est spes, id est, non cadit sub spe, nec amplius speratur. Quasi dicat : Spes ista non est de visibilibus et præsentibus bonis, sed est certa exspectatio futurorum invisibiliumque bonorum. Nam et fides (quæ utique de invisibilibus est) est substantia rerum sperandarum. Ideo additur : Nam quod videt quis, quid sperat? id est, quod jam in promptu habetur, et præsentialiter ac visibiliter adest, non magis speratur, sed potius possidetur. Si autem, id est quia, quæ non videmus, id est spiritualia et futura bona, speramus ; per patientiam exspectamus, id est, longanimiter ea præstolamur, non cedendo adversis, nec importune volentes dissolvi. Vel, Per patientiam, id est per adversitatum tolerantiam, exspectamus hanc consolationem. Nam tribulatio excitat nos ad futuræ consolationis actualem fiduciam.
paras.en: Moreover, we do not await this beatitude in vain. [[8:24|For we are saved by hope|Spe enim salvi facti sumus]], that is, by the act of hope, as by merit, we have been freed from guilt and made worthy of glory; for the act of virtue saves in this way. Or thus: *we are saved by hope*, that is, through the passion and merit of Christ we are already blessed and saved in hope, though not yet blessed in reality. Therefore we most surely await the aforesaid happiness. [[8:24|But hope|Spes autem]], that is, the thing hoped for, [[8:24|that is seen|quæ videtur]], that is, which is already present and obtained, [[8:24|is not hope|non est spes]], that is, does not fall under hope, and is no longer hoped for. As if to say: this hope is not of visible and present goods, but is the certain expectation of future and invisible goods. For faith too (which is of things unseen) [[Heb 11:1|is the substance of things to be hoped for|est substantia rerum sperandarum]]. Therefore it is added: [[8:24|For what a man seeth, why doth he hope for?|Nam quod videt quis, quid sperat]]? that is, what is already at hand, and present and visibly there, is no longer hoped for, but rather possessed. [[8:25|But if|Si autem]], that is, since, [[8:25|we hope for that which we see not|quod non videmus, speramus]], that is, spiritual and future goods, [[8:25|we wait for it with patience|per patientiam exspectamus]], that is, we await them with long-suffering, not yielding to adversity nor wishing importunately to be dissolved. Or, *with patience*, that is, by the bearing of adversities, we await this consolation. For tribulation stirs us to an actual confidence in future consolation.

paras.t: Consequenter docet Apostolus, quod non humana, sed divina virtute ac ope, ad prædictam felicitatem pertingimus. Similiter autem, id est, sicut per patientiam exspectamus bona futura, adjuti gratia Dei, simili modo pie ac gratiose spiritus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram. Locus iste usque ad illud, Scimus quoniam diligentibus Deum, dupliciter exponi potest : primo, de Spiritu Sancto ; secundo, de spiritu angelico.
paras.en: Next the Apostle teaches that it is not by human but by divine power and help that we reach the aforesaid happiness. [[8:26|Likewise|Similiter autem]], that is, as we await future goods with patience, helped by the grace of God, in like manner, kindly and graciously, [[8:26|the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity|spiritus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram]]. This passage, up to *And we know that to them that love God*, can be expounded in two ways: first, of the Holy Ghost; second, of an angelic spirit.

paras.t: Primo sic : Spiritus Sanctus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram, id est nos ipsos infirmitatibus spiritualibus plenos, illuminando intellectum, accendendo affectum. Nam quid oremus, sicut oportet, nescimus. Videtur huic contrarium. Aliqua enim sunt ex sua ratione honesta, virtuosa, et ad salutem necessaria, ut dilectio Dei et proximi, humilitas, pax, patientia. Talia autem scimus esse petenda a Deo. Scimus quoque quomodo sint petenda, videlicet indesinenter, et in nomine Christi ad gloriam Dei. Denique Christus nobis præfixit quid et quomodo orare oporteat, dicens : Sic ergo orabitis : Pater noster qui es in cœlis. Advertendum est itaque, quia (ut refert Valerius) opinio Socratis fuit, non debere nos ab immortalibus diis aliquid determinate postulare, quoniam ipsi melius scirent quam nos quid nobis expediat. Hoc autem sancti doctores reprobant propter duo : Primo, quia (ut tactum est) quædam sunt per se ad salutem necessaria, honesta et nobis præcepta. Talia ergo debemus petere determinate. Secundo, quoniam orando aliquid determinate, mens nostra pro illo magis accenditur, sicque capacior fit ejus quod poscit. Desiderium enim aperit capacemque facit affectum orantis. Quædam vero sunt indifferentia, quæ possunt saluti obesse sicut prodesse, ut sanitas corporis, cessatio tentationis, et multa hujusmodi. Talia non debemus determinate petere, nisi sub conditione beneplaciti Dei. Quia ergo in talibus sæpe decipimur, orantes quæ non proficiunt ad salutem, eo quod incertæ sint providentiæ nostræ, sicut et Paulus apostolus qui oravit stimulum carnis sibi auferri ; idcirco indigemus dirigi a Spiritu Sancto in petitione talium, ne petamus saluti contraria, vel aliter quam oportet. De his puto jam loqui Apostolum. Juxta quem sensum etiam a Sapiente scriptum est : Quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus ? et sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum tuum de cœlis?
paras.en: First thus: [[8:26|the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity|Spiritus Sanctus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram]], the Holy Spirit, that is, us ourselves, full of spiritual infirmities, by enlightening the understanding and kindling the affection. [[8:26|For, we know not what we should pray for as we ought|Nam quid oremus, sicut oportet, nescimus]]. This seems contrary to fact. For some things are of their very nature honourable, virtuous and necessary for salvation, as the love of God and neighbour[[Matt 22:37||]], humility[[Matt 11:29||]], peace, patience[[Luke 21:19||]]. Such things we know are to be asked of God. We know also how they are to be asked, namely without ceasing[[Luke 18:1||]], and in the name of Christ[[John 16:23||]], to the glory of God. Finally, Christ laid down for us what and how we ought to pray, saying: [[Matt 6:9|Thus therefore shall you pray: Our Father who art in heaven|Sic ergo orabitis : Pater noster qui es in cœlis]]. It must be noted, then, that (as Valerius relates) it was the opinion of Socrates that we ought not to ask anything determinate of the immortal gods, since they would know better than we what is good for us. The holy doctors reject this for two reasons. First, because (as was touched on) some things are of themselves necessary for salvation, honourable and commanded us; such things, therefore, we ought to ask for determinately. Second, because by praying for something determinately our mind is more kindled for it, and so becomes more capable of what it asks. For desire opens the affection of one who prays and makes it capable. But some things are indifferent, which can harm salvation as well as help it, such as bodily health, the ceasing of temptation, and many such. Such things we ought not to ask determinately, except under the condition of God's good pleasure. Since, then, we are often deceived in such things, praying for what does not profit salvation, because our providence is uncertain[[Wis 9:14||]] (as the apostle Paul too, who prayed that the sting of the flesh be taken from him[[2 Cor 12:8||]]), we therefore need to be directed by the Holy Ghost in asking for such things, lest we ask what is contrary to salvation, or otherwise than we ought. Of these, I think, the Apostle is here speaking. In which sense the Wise Man also wrote: [[Wis 9:13|who can think what the will of God is?|Quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus]]? and [[Wis 9:17|who shall know thy thought, except thou give wisdom, and send thy holy Spirit from above|sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum tuum de cœlis?]]?

paras.t: Si autem prædicta verba Apostoli universaliter dicta sunt, exponenda erunt hoc modo : Quid oremus, id est, quid decens a Domino postulemus (oratio enim est petitio decentium a Deo, secundum Damascenum), sicut oportet, cum circumstantiis debitis, nescimus propria virtute, sed nova illustratione egemus. Ideo subditur : sed ipse Spiritus Sanctus postulat pro nobis, id est, postulantes nos efficit vere salubria, gemitibus inenarrabilibus, id est suspiriis tam excessivis, tam pro liberatione præsentis exsilii, quam pro adeptione cœlestis paradisi, ut plene nequeant explicari. Dicitur autem Deus aliquid agere, non quia ipse immediate sic agit, sed quia facit nos sic agere, prout legitur in Exodo : Dominus dixit ad filios Israel : Jam nunc depone ornatum tuum, ut sciam quid faciam tibi. Abrahæ quoque dixit : Nunc cognovi quod timeas Dominum, id est, scire et cognoscere faciam. Qui autem scrutatur corda, id est quælibet divina Persona interiora corda conspiciens, scit quid desideret Spiritus, id est, approbat et exaudit quod Spiritus Sanctus desiderare nos facit. Quod enim ex immediata Spiritus Sancti inspiratione precamur, Domino placet, et exauditur ab eo, imo a Spiritu Sancto. Idem enim Spiritus orare nos facit, et orantes exaudit. Quia secundum Deum postulat, id est, quoniam Spiritus Sanctus facit nos postulare quæ Deo sunt placita, pro sanctis, id est pro nobis ipsis et aliis præordinatis ad vitam.
paras.en: But if the aforesaid words of the Apostle are said universally, they must be expounded thus: [[8:26|what we should pray for|Quid oremus]], that is, what fitting thing we should ask of the Lord (for prayer is the asking of fitting things from God, according to Damascene), [[8:26|as we ought|sicut oportet]], with the due circumstances, [[8:26|we know not|nescimus]] by our own power, but we need a new enlightening. Therefore it is added: [[8:26|but the Spirit himself asketh for us|sed ipse Spiritus Sanctus postulat pro nobis]], the Holy Spirit, that is, He makes us ask for things truly wholesome, [[8:26|with unspeakable groanings|gemitibus inenarrabilibus]], that is, with sighs so exceeding, both for deliverance from the present exile and for the gaining of the heavenly paradise, that they cannot be fully expressed. Now God is said to do something, not because He Himself does it so immediately, but because He makes us do so, as we read in Exodus: The Lord said to the children of Israel: [[Ex 33:5|Now presently lay aside thy ornaments, that I may know what to do to thee|Jam nunc depone ornatum tuum, ut sciam quid faciam tibi]]. And to Abraham He said: [[Gen 22:12|now I know that thou fearest God|Nunc cognovi quod timeas Dominum]], that is, I will make it known and recognized. [[8:27|And he that searcheth the hearts|Qui autem scrutatur corda]], that is, any divine Person beholding the inmost hearts, [[8:27|knoweth what the Spirit desireth|scit quid desideret Spiritus]], that is, approves and hears what the Holy Spirit makes us desire. For what we pray for by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Ghost pleases the Lord and is heard by Him, indeed by the Holy Ghost; for the same Spirit makes us pray and hears those who pray. [[8:27|because he asketh for the saints according to God|quia secundum Deum postulat pro sanctis]], that is, since the Holy Ghost makes us ask what is pleasing to God; *for the saints*, that is, for ourselves and others foreordained to life.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur sic : Spiritus angelicus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram, dæmones coercendo, gratiæ opem impetrando, et nobis fideliter tanquam piissimus custos ac diligens adsistendo. Nam quid oremus, sicut oportet, nescimus, secundum sensum prætactum ; sed ipse spiritus angelicus postulat pro nobis, orationes nostras offerens Domino : sicut Tobiæ Raphael aiebat, Quando orabas cum lacrimis, ego obtuli orationem tuam Deo. Et in Apocalypsi dicitur : Data sunt ei incensa multa, ut daret ea de orationibus Sanctorum super altare aureum, quod est ante thronum Dei. Gemitibus inenarrabilibus, id est vehementissimis quibusdam affectibus. Gemitus autem proprie sumptus non competit angelo, sed metaphorice tantum, sicut de Deo legitur : Tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus, etc. Qui autem scrutatur corda, id est Deus qui corda scrutatur, non inquirendo quod nescit, sed inspiciendo quod novit, scit quid desideret spiritus angelicus pro nostra salute; quia secundum Deum postulat pro sanctis : nam quum sit Deo beatifice inseparabiliterque unitus, nil cupit, nisi quod complaceat Domino.
paras.en: Second, it is expounded thus: [[8:26|the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity|Spiritus angelicus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram]], the angelic spirit, by restraining the demons, obtaining the help of grace, and standing by us faithfully as a most kind and diligent guardian. [[8:26|For, we know not what we should pray for as we ought|Nam quid oremus, sicut oportet, nescimus]], in the sense already touched on; [[8:26|but the Spirit himself asketh for us|sed ipse spiritus angelicus postulat pro nobis]], the angelic spirit, offering our prayers to the Lord: as Raphael said to Tobias, [[Tob 12:12|When thou didst pray with tears, and didst bury the dead, and didst leave thy dinner, and hide the dead by day in thy house, and bury them by night, I offered thy prayer to the Lord|Quando orabas cum lacrimis, et sepeliebas mortuos, et derelinquebas prandium tuum, et mortuos abscondebas per diem in domo tua, et nocte sepeliebas eos, ego obtuli orationem tuam]]. And in the Apocalypse it is said: [[Apoc 8:3|there was given to him much incense, that he should offer of the prayers of all saints, upon the golden altar which is before the throne of God|Data sunt ei incensa multa, ut daret ea de orationibus Sanctorum super altare aureum, quod est ante thronum Dei]]. [[8:26|with unspeakable groanings|Gemitibus inenarrabilibus]], that is, with certain most vehement affections. Groaning taken properly does not befit an angel, but only metaphorically, as is read of God: [[Gen 6:6|being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart|Tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus]], etc. [[8:27|And he that searcheth the hearts|Qui autem scrutatur corda]], that is, God who searches hearts, not by inquiring into what He knows not, but by beholding what He knows[[Wis 1:6||]] [the margin note here is hard to read (it looks like Sap. vi or xi); Denis quotes nothing; Wis 1:6, "a searcher of his heart", is offered as the likeliest place], [[8:27|knoweth what the Spirit desireth|scit quid desideret spiritus]], the angelic spirit, for our salvation; [[8:27|because he asketh for the saints according to God|quia secundum Deum postulat pro sanctis]]: for since he is blessedly and inseparably united to God, he desires nothing but what is pleasing to the Lord.

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit Apostolus proprietatem eorum qui æternam beatitudinem obtinebunt. Scimus autem quoniam diligentibus Deum caritate infusa et supernaturali ac perseveranti, omnia, tam bona quam mala, prospera et adversa, cooperantur finaliter in bonum felicitatis æternæ, quia per hæc aliquo modo proficiscuntur ad Dominum. Bona enim, id est opera virtuosa, cooperantur eis in bonum directe, mala vero indirecte. Nam ubi abundavit iniquitas, abundavit et gratia. Ideo scriptum est de viro justo : Omnia quæcumque faciet, prosperabuntur. Sæpe enim contingit, ut quo se gravius peccasse perpendunt, eo humiliores et ferventiores reddantur. His qui secundum propositum voluntatis divinæ, vel secundum rationem prædestinationis æternæ, vocati sunt sancti, id est, Deo operante ad Sanctorum pertinent sortem. Vel, Secundum propositum, id est divinæ mentis decretum, vocati sunt sancti, id est, ad gratiam sanctificantem deducti sunt, ita ut re et nomine veraciter sancti dicantur, gratiamque perseverantem ac finalem, quæ solis electis præstatur, adipiscantur.
paras.en: Next the Apostle shows the mark of those who will obtain eternal beatitude. [[8:28|And we know that to them that love God|Scimus autem quoniam diligentibus Deum]] with infused, supernatural and persevering charity, [[8:28|all things|omnia]], good as well as evil, prosperous and adverse, [[8:28|work together|cooperantur]] in the end [[8:28|unto good|in bonum]] of eternal happiness, because through these they advance in some way toward the Lord. For good things, that is, virtuous works, work together for their good directly, but evil things indirectly. For [[Rom 5:20|where sin abounded, grace did more abound|ubi abundavit iniquitas, abundavit et gratia]]. Therefore it is written of the just man: [[Ps 1:3|all whatsoever he shall do shall prosper|Omnia quæcumque faciet, prosperabuntur]]. For it often happens that the more gravely they consider themselves to have sinned, the more humble and fervent they are made. [[8:28|to such as, according to his purpose|His qui secundum propositum]] of the divine will, or according to the order of eternal predestination, [[8:28|are called to be saints|vocati sunt sancti]], that is, by God's working they belong to the lot of the Saints. Or, *according to his purpose*, that is, the decree of the divine mind, *are called to be saints*, that is, have been brought to sanctifying grace, so that they are truly called saints in fact and in name, and obtain persevering and final grace, which is given to the elect alone.

paras.t: Nam quos præscivit, id est, ab æterno prænovit ad vitam, et per approbationem, sicut ad Moysen loquitur : Scio te ex nomine ; et prædestinavit, id est, in sua æterna dispositione præmisit atque præordinavit, conformes fieri, per gratiam adoptionis, imaginis Filii sui, id est Filio suo naturali, qui est imago Patris sui, quum sit imago bonitatis paternæ, candor æternæ lucis, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis. Filiatio enim adoptiva electorum, est similitudo filiationis naturalis divinæ. Conformantur ergo prædestinati Filio Dei, quum fiunt filii adoptivi : quia per gratiam gratum facientem, et cetera dona Spiritus Sancti sortiuntur quamdam supernaturalem assimilationem cum Deo Patre, cujus Filius est imago. Assimilantur quoque et Filio, qui est Verbum, veritas et sapientia Patris, quum natura eorum intellectualis divinorum contemplatione perficitur. Potest quoque referri conformatio ista ad Filium secundum naturam ejus assumptam. Sic enim prædestinati sunt conformes fieri imaginis Filii Dei, ut sint coheredes Christi, et sicut portaverunt imaginem terreni, sic portent imaginem cœlestis.
paras.en: [[8:29|For whom he foreknew|Nam quos præscivit]], that is, foreknew from eternity unto life, and by approval, as He says to Moses: [[Ex 33:12|I know thee by name|Scio te ex nomine]][[Ex 33:17||]]; [[8:29|he also predestinated|et prædestinavit]], that is, in His eternal disposition He sent before and foreordained, [[8:29|to be made conformable|conformes fieri]], by the grace of adoption, [[8:29|to the image of his Son|imaginis Filii sui]], that is, to His natural Son, who is the image of His Father[[Col 1:15||]], since He is [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty, and the image of his goodness|imago bonitatis paternæ, candor æternæ lucis, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis]] [Denis puts "the image of his goodness" first]. For the adoptive sonship of the elect is a likeness of the natural divine sonship. The predestined, therefore, are conformed to the Son of God when they become adopted sons: because through sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God] and the other gifts of the Holy Ghost they obtain a certain supernatural likeness to God the Father, whose image the Son is. They are likened also to the Son, who is the Word[[John 1:1||]], the truth[[John 14:6||]] and the wisdom[[1 Cor 1:24||]] of the Father, when their intellectual nature is perfected by the contemplation of divine things. This conformity may also be referred to the Son according to His assumed nature. For so are the predestined to be made conformable to the image of the Son of God, that they may be joint heirs with Christ, and [[1 Cor 15:49|as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly|sicut portaverunt imaginem terreni, sic portent imaginem cœlestis]].

paras.t: Ut sit ipse Filius Dei primogenitus in multis fratribus, id est, inter prædestinatos fideles, qui fratres ejus sunt secundum naturam assumptam, primatum tenens, ordinem dignitatis, tanquam caput eorum, et jus primogenituræ possidens, hereditatem Patris abundantius percipiendo, eamque aliis distribuendo. Dicitur etiam Christus primogenitus mortuorum, quoniam propria potestate surrexit, et erat primus impassibilis resurgens. Porro, ut unigenitus, non habet fratres : sic enim est unicus Filius, verusque Deus. Sed ut primogenitus, fratres habet : quorum ipse naturam assumpsit, et qui suæ gloriæ participes erunt. Unde ad Hebræos habetur : Non confunditur eos fratres vocare, dicens : Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis. Nam et in Evangelio loquens dilectæ discipulæ : Vade, inquit, dic fratribus meis.
paras.en: [[8:29|that he might be the Firstborn amongst many brethren|Ut sit ipse Filius Dei primogenitus in multis fratribus]], He, the Son of God, that is, among the predestined faithful, who are His brethren according to the assumed nature, holding the primacy[[Col 1:18||]], the rank of dignity, as their head, and possessing the right of the firstborn, receiving the Father's inheritance more abundantly and distributing it to others. Christ is also called [[Apoc 1:5|the first begotten of the dead|primogenitus mortuorum]], since He rose by His own power and was the first to rise impassible. Now as Only-begotten He has no brethren: for so He is the only Son and true God. But as Firstborn He has brethren: those whose nature He assumed, and who will share His glory. Hence it is said to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:11|he is not ashamed to call them brethren, saying|Non confunditur eos fratres vocare, dicens]]: [[Heb 2:12|I will declare thy name to my brethren|Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis]][[Ps 21:23||]]. For in the Gospel too, speaking to the beloved disciple [Mary Magdalen], He says: [[John 20:17|go to my brethren|Vade, inquit, dic fratribus meis]].

paras.t: Hoc autem sciendum, quod præscientia non sumitur hic sicut communiter sumitur, ut dum reprobi dicuntur præsciti, videlicet prout prædestinationi opponitur; sed sumitur jam prout est quasi via sive præambulum ad prædestinationem. Quum enim Deus nil agat casu aut ignoranter, oportet notionem secundum ordinem rationis præcedere prædestinationem. Ad insinuandum ergo quod Deus non eligit nisi præcognitos, ait Apostolus : Nam quos præscivit, et prædestinavit.
paras.en: Now this must be known, that foreknowledge is not taken here as it is commonly taken, as when the reprobate are called the *foreknown*, namely as it is opposed to predestination; but it is taken here as a kind of way or preamble to predestination. For since God does nothing by chance or in ignorance, knowledge must, in the order of reason, precede predestination. To intimate, then, that God elects none but those foreknown, the Apostle says: [[8:29|For whom he foreknew, he also predestinated|Nam quos præscivit, et prædestinavit]].

paras.t: Quæ autem bona prædestinationem sequantur, ostendit Apostolus. Quos autem prædestinavit ab æterno, hos et vocavit ad statum salutis, ad fidem et gratiam, vel per inspirationem internam, vel per instructionem angelicam, vel per prædicationem humanam. Et quos vocavit, hos et justificavit, indulgentiam conferendo, et gratiam infundendo. Quos autem justificavit, illos et magnificavit, exaltando eos in gloria. Quosdam enim jam magnificavit hoc modo, alios magnificabit. Itaque prædestinatio gratiam præparat, respicitque gratiæ bonum finale ; vocatio gratiam offert, et retrahit a malo; justificatio gratiam confert, et respicit bonum gratiæ initiale; magnificatio gratiam consummat in gloria, et concernit futurum bonum felicitatis æternæ. Horum quatuor, prædestinatio est in Deo, alia tria in nobis sunt. Si ergo prædestinatus es, quamvis avertaris a Deo et fugias, tamen vocaris; quamvis pecces, tamen justificaris ; quamvis moriaris, tamen ad impassibilem vitam transfereris.
paras.en: What goods follow predestination the Apostle shows. [[8:30|And whom he predestinated|Quos autem prædestinavit]] from eternity, [[8:30|them he also called|hos et vocavit]] to the state of salvation, to faith and grace, whether by inward inspiration, or by angelic instruction, or by human preaching. [[8:30|And whom he called, them he also justified|Et quos vocavit, hos et justificavit]], by granting pardon and infusing grace. [[8:30|And whom he justified, them he also glorified|Quos autem justificavit, illos et magnificavit]] [Denis's text reads *magnificavit*, "magnified"; the edition notes the Vulgate *glorificavit*], by exalting them in glory. For some He has already magnified in this way, others He will magnify. Thus predestination prepares grace, and regards the final good of grace; calling offers grace and draws back from evil; justification confers grace, and regards the initial good of grace; magnification consummates grace in glory, and concerns the future good of eternal happiness. Of these four, predestination is in God, the other three are in us. If therefore thou art predestined, though thou turn away from God and flee, yet thou art called; though thou sin, yet thou art justified; though thou die, yet thou art carried over to impassible life.

paras.t: Quid ergo dicemus ad hæc? id est, quomodo ista satis mirari, quomodo tantam gratiam satis laudare poterimus? Si Deus pro nobis est, nosque defendit : sicut est pro prædestinatis ; quis contra nos? id est, quis nobis nocere valebit? Nullus utique, quia omnia cooperabuntur nobis in bonum. Si enim tentemur a dæmone, si insectemur a mundo, per Dei gratiam omnia fiunt nobis materia meritorum : imo si corpus occidatur, anima per patientiam coronatur. Ideo sanctus Job ait : Pone me juxta te, et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me. Qui Deus Pater, inter alia beneficia sua nobis impensa, etiam proprio Filio suo incarnato non pepercit, liberando eum a mortis angustia, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum manibus adversariorum permissive ; electis vero dedit eum effective, juxta quod scriptum est, Parvulus natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis. Secundum B. Thomam in tertia parte, Deus tradidit Christum triplici modo : Primo, quia ab æterno præordinavit per Christi passionem mundum esse salvandum. Secundo, quoniam inspiravit ei voluntatem patiendi pro nobis : et ita voluit Christum pati per modum præcepti, cui Filius libentissime obedivit. Tertio permissive, ut dictum est. Quomodo non etiam cum illo omnia nobis donavit? Per locum a majori concluditur, quod quia Filium suum sibi coæternum, consubstantialem et coæqualem dedit nobis, etiam cetera omnia minora Filio suo præstiterit nobis, quantum ad salutem requiritur. Angelos enim dedit nobis in concives atque custodes; omnia corporalia subjecit fidelibus; omnem gratiam in præsenti, omnem gloriam in futuro dare paratus est, sicut et Filius contestatur : Si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis, ut gaudium vestrum sit plenum.
paras.en: [[8:31|What shall we then say to these things?|Quid ergo dicemus ad hæc]]? that is, how shall we be able to wonder enough at these things, how praise enough so great a grace? [[8:31|If God be for us|Si Deus pro nobis]], and defends us, as He is for the predestined, [[8:31|who is against us|quis contra nos]]? that is, who will be able to harm us? No one at all, because all things will work together for our good. For if we are tempted by the devil, if we are persecuted by the world, through God's grace all things become matter of merit for us: indeed if the body is slain, the soul is crowned through patience. Therefore holy Job says: [[Job 17:3|set me beside thee, and let any man's hand fight against me|Pone me juxta te, et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me]]. [[8:32|He that spared not even his own Son|Qui etiam proprio Filio suo non pepercit]]: God the Father, among His other benefits bestowed on us, spared not even His own incarnate Son, by freeing Him from the anguish of death, [[8:32|but delivered him up for us all|sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum]] into the hands of His adversaries permissively; but to the elect He gave Him effectively, according to what is written: [[Is 9:6|For a CHILD IS BORN to us, and a son is given to us|Parvulus natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis]]. According to blessed Thomas in the third part [of the *Summa*], God delivered Christ in three ways: first, because from eternity He preordained that the world was to be saved by Christ's passion; second, because He inspired Him with the will to suffer for us, and so willed Christ to suffer by way of a command, which the Son most willingly obeyed; third, permissively, as has been said. [[8:32|how hath he not also, with him, given us all things?|Quomodo non etiam cum illo omnia nobis donavit]]? By an argument from the greater it is concluded that, since He gave us His Son, coeternal, consubstantial and coequal with Himself, He has also bestowed on us all other things, lesser than His Son, so far as is required for salvation. For He has given us the angels as fellow citizens and guardians; He has subjected all bodily things to the faithful; He is ready to give all grace in the present and all glory in the future, as the Son also testifies: [[John 16:23|if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you|Si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis]], [[John 16:24|that your joy may be full|ut gaudium vestrum sit plenum]].

paras.t: Omnia verba hæc divini Apostoli affectuosissima atque dulcissima sunt, et tota cordis intentione ac devotione pensanda.
paras.en: All these words of the divine Apostle are most full of affection and most sweet, and are to be weighed with the whole attention and devotion of the heart.

paras.t: Quis accusabit adversus electos Dei? Quasi dicat : Nullius accusatio poterit eis coram Deo nocere in hora mortis vel in die judicii. Possunt tamen jam fraterne accusari a proximis, et paterne corrigi a prælatis. Hinc enim scriptum est : Projectus est draco magnus, serpens antiquus accusator fratrum nostrorum. Quod autem nemo poterit eos accusare, patet, quoniam Deus est qui justificat eos : idcirco, Quis est qui condemnet eos? An Christus Jesus qui mortuus est pro eis salvandis, imo qui et resurrexit tertia die, qui est ad dexteram Dei residens? Christus secundum divinam naturam, dicitur esse a dextris Patris, id est in summo honore et Patris æqualitate. Secundum humanitatem vero, est ad dexteram Patris, id est in potioribus bonis ejus. Unde ipse ait : Ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus.
paras.en: [[8:33|Who shall accuse against the elect of God?|Quis accusabit adversus electos Dei]]? As if to say: no one's accusation can harm them before God in the hour of death or on the day of judgement. Yet they may now be accused in a brotherly way by their neighbours, and corrected in a fatherly way by their prelates. For hence it is written: [[Apoc 12:9|that great dragon was cast out, that old serpent|Projectus est draco magnus, serpens antiquus]], [[Apoc 12:10|the accuser of our brethren|accusator fratrum nostrorum]]. That no one can accuse them is plain, because [[8:33|God is he that justifieth|Deus est qui justificat]] them: therefore, [[8:34|Who is he that shall condemn|Quis est qui condemnet]] them? Shall [[8:34|Christ Jesus that died|Christus Jesus qui mortuus est]] to save them, [[8:34|yea that is risen also again|imo qui et resurrexit]] on the third day, [[8:34|who is at the right hand of God|qui est ad dexteram Dei]], seated there? Christ according to His divine nature is said to be at the right hand of the Father, that is, in the highest honour and in equality with the Father. But according to His humanity He is at the right hand of the Father, that is, in His more excellent goods. Hence He Himself says: [[Apoc 3:21|have overcome and am set down with my Father in his throne|Ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]].

paras.t: Qui etiam interpellat pro nobis, ut mediator Dei et hominum. Scriptum est enim : Advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum justum. Secundum quosdam, Christus interpellat pro nobis, non voce, sed miseratione ac repræsentatione, dum indesinenter naturam quam pro nobis assumpsit, et diram mortem quam pertulit, Patris vultui offert. Ut enim ait Bernardus : Mater ostendit Filio pectus et ubera : Filius ostendit Patri latus et vulnera : nec potest esse repulsa, ubi tot concurrunt amoris insignia. Verumtamen, quum ad Hebræos dicat Apostolus : Christus sempiternum habet sacerdotium, unde et salvare potest in perpetuum, accedens per semetipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro nobis ; non videtur cur Christo ut mediatori non competat voce interpellare pro nobis. Denique, oratio est explicatio desiderii, et interpres ac nuntia voluntatis. Secundum Augustinum quoque, illud licet orare quod licet desiderare. Quum ergo Christus nostram salutem desideret, et ob id Patri latus ac vulnera repræsentet, ut nostri misereatur : cur non voce explicet hanc voluntatem, pro nobis orando? Et quum ipse magis cupiat nostram salutem, quam aliquis Beatorum, cur non orat vocaliter eo modo quo virgo Maria, vel ceteri Sancti? Si autem ideo dicatur non orare vocaliter, quia non est opportuna in patria vocalis oratio, eadem ratione nec Virgo beata oraret vocaliter, nec Christus in hoc sæculo orasset voce pro nobis.
paras.en: [[8:34|who also maketh intercession for us|Qui etiam interpellat pro nobis]], as mediator of God and men. For it is written: [[1 John 2:1|we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just|Advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum justum]]. According to some, Christ intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion and by presenting, in that He unceasingly offers before the Father's face the nature He assumed for us and the cruel death He bore. For as Bernard says: The Mother shows the Son her breast and paps; the Son shows the Father His side and wounds: nor can there be a refusal where so many tokens of love concur. Yet since the Apostle says to the Hebrews: Christ [[Heb 7:24|hath an everlasting priesthood|sempiternum habet sacerdotium]], [[Heb 7:25|Whereby he is able also to save for ever them that come to God by him; always living to make intercession for us|unde et salvare potest in perpetuum, accedens per semetipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro nobis]], it does not appear why it should not befit Christ as mediator to intercede for us by voice. Moreover, prayer is the expression of desire, the interpreter and messenger of the will. According to Augustine too, it is lawful to pray for what it is lawful to desire. Since, then, Christ desires our salvation, and for that reason presents His side and wounds to the Father that He may have mercy on us, why should He not express this will in words, by praying for us? And since He desires our salvation more than any of the Blessed, why does He not pray vocally in the way the Virgin Mary or the other Saints do? And if it be said that He does not pray vocally because vocal prayer is not fitting in the fatherland, by the same reason neither would the blessed Virgin pray vocally, nor would Christ in this world have prayed for us with His voice.

paras.t: Itaque quum Deus tantam nobis caritatem ostenderit, et tanta bona per Christum largitus sit. Quis ergo nos separabit a caritate actuali vel habituali Christi secundum utramque ejus naturam? Num quid tribulatio corporis? an angustia, id est afflictio mentis? an fames? an nuditas, id est vestimentorum inopia? an persecutio, quæ est de loco ad locum? an periculum, id est apparatus mortis? an gladius, id est mors ipsa? Tanquam dicat : Nullum horum separare nos poterit.
paras.en: Since, therefore, God has shown us so great charity, and bestowed such great goods through Christ: [[8:35|Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ?|Quis ergo nos separabit a caritate Christi?]], love actual or habitual, of Christ according to both His natures? [[8:35|Shall tribulation|tribulatio]] of the body? [[8:35|Or distress|an angustia]], that is, affliction of the mind? [[8:35|Or famine|an fames]]? [[8:35|Or nakedness|an nuditas]], that is, want of clothing? [[8:35|Or persecution|an persecutio]], which is from place to place? [[8:35|Or danger|an periculum]], that is, the preparing of death? [[8:35|Or the sword|an gladius]], that is, death itself? As if to say: none of these will be able to separate us.

paras.t: Sicut scriptum est in persona justorum seu martyrum adversa patientium, scilicet pœnas prætactas : Quoniam propter te, id est propter tui amorem, et quia coram hominibus te confitemur, nec a justitiæ tuæ via recedere volumus ; vel, Propter te finaliter, id est, ut te Deum pro præmio acquiramus ; mortificamur tota die, id est, assidue tribulamur, atque per quotidianas persecutiones et adversitates ad mortem deducimur; vel certe quia nos ipsos quotidie mortificamus, orando, lugendo, abstinendo, contra proprias concupiscentias præliando, propriam voluntatem fraudando, et in ceteris virtutum exercitiis ac pœnitentiæ laboribus desudando ; æstimati, id est a persecutoribus et perversis hominibus reputati et spreti, sumus ut oves occisionis, id est sicut oves quæ occiduntur ut lana eorum et carnes in usum occidentium veniant. Unde et Christus ait discipulis : Ecce ego mitto vos sicut oves in medio luporum ; et alibi, Venit hora, ut omnis qui interficit vos, arbitretur obsequium se præstare Deo.
